# CHAPTER 171

## THE SUPPER PLAYER

Rinna asked the question I had not.

"How much is the yard?"

I stopped.

She was standing beside the second wagon with one hand inside the food
sack and the other holding an apple that had gone soft on one side.

"I don't know."

"Food before or after?"

"After."

"Horses?"

"No."

"How long?"

"Twenty minutes."

"Pay?"

"One silver two. Half before. Half after."

Marek looked up from tying his shoe.

"One silver two?"

"It was three."

"I remember three."

"So does Harel."

"Does he remember where he put it?"

"Musicians."

Marek sat back.

"I dislike music."

Serra, beside the wagon, said, "You sing."

"I perform melody."

"You shout on pitch sometimes."

"Exactly."

Rinna ignored them.

"When?"

"After second course. Before speeches."

"What time is second course?"

"I don't know."

She looked at me.

"I carried the terms."

"You carried some terms."

"Apparently."

Davin came around the front wagon.

"Horses?"

"Not included."

He looked at Rinna.

She nodded.

He said, "Need oats."

"How much?"

"Tonight."

That was not a number.

It was enough for her.

Rinna bit the good side of the apple and pointed at the cooper's shed.

"Yard is two copper until morning. Water included. No hay. No sleeping
in the shed."

"Why?"

"Cooper."

That also explained nothing.

It did not need to.

Teren arrived before we finished deciding whether one silver two was
good.

He had Harel's half payment.

Rinna took it, checked it, and put it away.

Marek watched the silver disappear into her purse.

"There it goes."

"It was never yours," Rinna said.

"It could have been emotionally."

"It wasn't."

Teren looked around.

"Founder Hall in an hour. Nessa, Pell, Serra, Marek, Greg, Orin, Iven."

"What are we doing?" Marek asked.

"Deciding."

"You already decided."

"Then we're confirming."

That was apparently different.

We walked back into the old center carrying almost nothing.

Pell had the small prop basket. Iven carried two folded costume pieces.
Nessa carried a third over her arm and would not let anybody else touch
it. I had my crutches and no assigned object.

This made me suspicious.

Founder Hall was worse with people in it.

Not guests.

Workers.

The clear strip at the end of the hall had disappeared beneath stacked
serving boards. Three long baskets of bread sat against the wall.
Someone had found the green tablecloths, which meant somebody else was
now arguing about why there were only eleven.

Harel stood near the fireplace.

Teren said, "Space."

Harel pointed to the far end.

A woman carrying a tray said, "No."

Harel looked at her.

"We need the end."

"So do we."

"For twenty minutes."

"After second course?"

"Yes."

"Then after second course you can have it."

Teren looked at the stacked boards.

"Where do those go?"

"Kitchen."

"When?"

"When they're empty."

Harel said, "There."

The woman said, "After."

Teren nodded.

"After."

Harel seemed annoyed that this had been solved without him.

We went to look.

I had thought the side door would work for the Sword.

It was broad enough. The floor outside was level. There was a short
passage to the yard.

"That," I said.

The tray woman had followed us.

"No."

"Why?"

"Plates."

The passage was empty.

I looked at it.

She pointed through the door.

"Plates."

"I don't see any."

"You will."

Teren said, "Other door?"

"Coal."

"Gallery?"

"Food."

"Front?"

"Guests."

I said, "Fireplace?"

Everybody looked at the fireplace.

It was large enough to roast something I would have preferred not to
meet alive.

Nessa said, "No."

"I wasn't suggesting inside it."

"Heat."

"Yes."

Pell touched the wall near it.

Nessa slapped his hand away.

"Hot."

"I know now."

The woman with the tray pointed to a narrow space beside the second
table.

"After plates, you can come through there."

"With the board?" Teren asked.

"What board?"

That took us back to the wagons.

Not physically.

Argumentatively.

Teren had wanted Sword.

Nessa did not want the mounting cloth near food.

Pell said the board could come through the front if guests were not
seated yet.

Harel said guests would be seated.

I said I could mount outside and come in through the side door.

The tray woman said, "Plates."

Teren looked at me.

I said, "I know."

"No Sword."

That was it.

Marek said, "You traveled a day and a half to be unemployed."

"I'm still here."

"Decoratively."

Teren looked at the hall again.

"King. Shopkeeper. Widow."

"Twenty minutes?" Serra asked.

"Less if speeches start."

"Whose speeches?"

Harel said, "Founding addresses."

Marek brightened.

"How long?"

Harel's face changed.

"Scheduled?"

"Yes."

"How long?"

"Forty minutes."

Marek smiled.

Harel said, "The speeches stay where they are. I've already moved them twice for the musicians."

"I hadn't proposed anything."

"Then we agree."

The musicians arrived while we were still in the hall.

There were four of them. Two women, two men. Fiddle, narrow drum, a
little reed instrument, and something with strings that sat across one
woman's lap.

They knew where they were going.

That was the first thing I noticed.

The second was that Harel stopped looking irritated for almost ten
seconds when he saw them.

"Gallery until doors," he told them. "Then front corner. First course,
low. Between courses, whatever keeps them from talking too loudly."

The fiddler nodded.

"Speech?"

"Stop."

"After?"

"Depends."

That was their negotiation.

One of the women looked at us.

"Players?"

Marek bowed.

"Melody."

She looked at him.

"No."

Serra laughed.

The musicians went upstairs.

A few minutes later, the lap instrument sounded.

The note was too clean.

Not loud. Clean.

It carried through the hall and seemed to settle under the rafters
before it faded.

I looked up.

Pell did too.

"Wire?" he asked.

Nessa said, "Charm."

The musician plucked another note.

This one seemed to come from farther down the hall than she was.

Not much farther.

Enough.

I looked at Teren.

He was talking to Harel.

Nobody else had stopped.

The third note spread differently again, soft near us, clearer toward
the doors.

The musician adjusted a small silver clip on the instrument's frame.

Then she played normally.

Fantasy returned to the room as if it had never left.

Not a miracle.

Not a secret.

A working woman adjusting how her instrument carried in a bad hall.

I wanted to ask.

I did not.

Pell whispered, "Sound veil."

Nessa said, "No. Throw."

"Same family."

"No."

"Close."

"No."

That was all I got.

Teren clapped once.

"Back."

We went to the wagons.

I thought about the silver clip for most of the walk.

Then Davin made me move because I was standing where he needed to carry
oats.

The rest of the afternoon belonged to people who had jobs.

Nessa and Pell chose clothes.

Serra disappeared for nearly an hour and came back with two apples and
no explanation.

Orin found a barber.

I knew because his beard was shorter when he returned.

Marek went into town with Iven and came back carrying a small paper
twist of roasted nuts.

He offered me one.

I took two.

"Thief."

"Travel costs."

"That joke is old."

"So are your nuts."

He took the bag away.

I washed.

Changed my shirt.

Checked the clasp.

Put my coat back on.

At Founder Hall, guests were arriving.

Founding Week had apparently given everyone permission to wear green.

Not everyone did.

Enough did that the room looked as though somebody had scattered leaves
among the tables.

Small potted trees stood near the walls. Apple branches had been cut and
tied above the fireplace. Three old wooden barrels sat beside the front
table, polished enough that nobody was going to drink from them.

A man near the door was explaining to a child that one barrel had
belonged to the first pressing house.

The child asked if it still had cider.

The man said no.

The child lost interest.

I understood the child.

We were put in a narrow room off the passage behind the hall.

It had once been storage and had not entirely changed its mind.

There were shelves.

Two broken chairs.

A sack of onions.

Nessa moved the onions.

A kitchen boy moved them back.

Nessa moved our clothes instead.

"His room," she said.

"Onions?" Pell asked.

"Apparently."

The first course began.

We could hear it.

Plates.

The tray woman had been right.

The side passage became a river of people carrying food.

Bowls went in.

Empty bowls came out.

Bread went in.

A broken cup came out in pieces.

One server stood in the passage for three seconds swearing at a stain on
her sleeve, then disappeared again.

The musicians played softly from the front corner.

The sound reached us oddly.

Sometimes clear.

Sometimes covered by plates.

Once the fiddle seemed to come from the passage behind me.

I turned.

Nothing.

Pell saw.

"Throw."

Nessa said, "Eat your onion."

"I don't have an onion."

"Find one."

I asked, "How does it work?"

Nessa was pinning Marek's collar.

"What?"

"The sound."

"Prepared clip."

"I saw that."

"Then you know."

"No."

"Good."

Marek said, "This is why people don't teach you things."

"Nobody taught you your collar."

"Royal instinct."

Nessa pushed his chin up.

"Royal stillness."

He became still.

I looked toward the hall again.

The sound had moved.

Or I thought it had.

That was the interesting part.

I could not tell whether the instrument was making sound somewhere else
or making me judge the source wrong.

Those were different things.

I knew enough now to know that different mattered.

I also knew enough to leave it alone while we were working.

The first course ended.

The musicians played louder.

People talked louder anyway.

The second course arrived in large covered dishes that smelled of pork,
apples, onions, and something sweet.

We had not eaten since morning beyond nuts.

Marek watched a platter pass.

"I can perform hungry."

Serra said, "You've done everything hungry."

"Exactly. Experience."

Teren came in.

"King. Short. Shopkeeper. Widow. Greg, you're Shopkeeper only."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Probably."

He looked at me.

"Not a promise."

"Good."

He left.

Second course took longer than Harel expected.

We knew because Harel came through the passage three times.

The first time he said, "Ten minutes."

The second time he said, "Seven."

The third time he said, "Ready."

Teren asked, "How long?"

"Twenty."

"You found time?"

"I stole it from the third speaker."

From the hall, somebody called, "Harel!"

He closed his eyes.

"Ready."

Then he left.

The serving boards came out.

The clear end of the hall appeared.

Not all at once.

Workers carried boards, baskets, cloths, and one enormous pot through
the side passage.

We stayed against the wall.

I did not need to be told.

Pell did.

The tray woman pointed at him.

"Wall."

He moved.

When the last board cleared, Teren looked into the hall.

"Go."

Marek went.

No crown.

No platform.

No scenery.

He walked into a room of seventy-something people who were still
drinking cider and talking about pork.

"I have been told," he said, "that this town was founded."

A man at the nearest table said, "Allegedly."

Marek stopped.

"Sir."

"King."

"You accept my authority."

"No."

The table laughed.

That helped.

The next table noticed.

Serra entered before Marek could make the man his entire kingdom.

The King piece was short enough that I could hear its shape from the
passage.

Not every word.

Shape.

Marek took the room slowly.

Serra cut him whenever he began enjoying himself too much.

The musicians sat near the wall with their instruments down.

One of them was eating bread.

They watched some.

Talked quietly during some.

Workers.

When King ended, the room applauded.

Not wildly.

Enough.

Shopkeeper was next.

Iven went first.

Then me.

The hall was harder than the market and easier than the arcade.

Nobody left.

That did not mean they listened.

A woman at the second table was still telling a story when I entered.

A man near the fireplace had turned his chair toward somebody behind
him.

Two children were trading pieces of apple under the table.

Iven began the debt.

I answered.

The first exchange landed nowhere.

I could feel myself wanting to push.

Louder.

Sharper.

Make them look.

Then a cup fell.

It hit stone and did not break.

Half the room looked at the cup.

I waited.

The server picked it up.

She looked at me.

"Sorry."

I said, "Add it to his debt."

The room came back.

Iven looked offended.

"I didn't drop it."

"Your account is complicated."

"I wasn't near it."

"That has never protected anyone."

The merchant table laughed first.

I knew it was the merchant table because somebody had said cooperage
prices there during second course.

Or maybe they were coopers.

I did not know.

The rest followed enough.

Iven said, "I refuse responsibility."

"Excellent. Responsibility charges extra."

That worked.

I almost reached for something older.

Jurisdiction.

Employment.

A line that had paid before.

I felt it.

Then let it go.

Iven gave me something new instead.

"What if I leave town?"

I looked at the old wall through the open door.

"I've seen your road."

A few people groaned.

That was better than laughter.

It belonged here.

We finished.

I got out.

No bow that lasted too long.

No waiting for another laugh.

Widow followed.

Serra and Orin did less.

That was why it worked.

The room had been asked to listen twice already.

They made it listen smaller.

Orin's widow debt became a cider press instead of a chair because there
were three ceremonial barrels sitting behind him and apparently he had
eyes.

Serra said, "You sold my husband's press?"

"Only the useful half."

"Which half?"

"The half your husband wasn't using."

"He is dead."

"Exactly."

An older woman near the front laughed so hard she coughed.

Her neighbor hit her back.

Orin waited.

Serra waited.

The woman waved at them to continue.

They did.

Teren appeared at the passage.

Two fingers.

Two minutes.

Orin saw him.

Serra saw him.

They cut something.

I did not know what.

The ending arrived cleanly.

Applause.

Then Harel walked directly into it.

"Thank you. Master Ennet will now speak on the charter stones."

That was the end of us.

No encore.

No second bow.

No one more thing.

A gray-haired man stood.

The room turned away from us.

We cleared the end before he finished his first sentence.

I liked that.

Not emotionally.

Practically.

We had twenty minutes.

Then Rellin had itself back.

Harel did not pay us immediately.

Of course he did not.

He was standing beside the front table whispering to a woman who had
apparently become furious about the order of speakers.

Teren waited.

Rinna had arrived for the meal and the money.

She waited too.

The first speaker talked about stones.

The second talked about the first orchard planted beyond the old wall.

The third had lost time to us and seemed determined to recover it
through density.

Marek whispered, "We stole from this?"

"Be grateful," Serra said.

"I am."

The musicians began packing quietly.

The woman with the lap instrument removed the silver clip.

I watched.

She noticed.

I looked away too late.

"Actor?" she whispered.

"Sometimes."

She held up the clip.

"Throw clasp."

"Pell said throw."

"Pell was right."

Nessa, behind me, said, "Rare."

The musician smiled.

I asked, "It moves the sound?"

"Some."

"Or where people think it comes from?"

Her smile changed.

"Those aren't always different."

That was not an answer.

It was worse.

"How much mana?"

She looked at me more carefully.

"Not much. Prepared work does most of it."

"Prepared by you?"

"No."

Before I could ask who, somebody at the front shushed us.

The third speaker was still speaking.

The musician leaned closer.

"Buy one if you want one."

"Where?"

"Instrument maker."

"Here?"

She nodded toward the square.

"Blue shutters. Ask for Varo."

Then she put the clasp into a padded box and went back to packing.

I did not go to Varo.

Not then.

Harel finally paid.

The second half of one silver two disappeared into Rinna's purse beside
the first.

Teren said, "Done."

Harel said, "On time."

That seemed to be praise.

Then Harel was gone because somebody had put the wrong cider at the
front table.

We ate in the kitchen yard after the speeches began.

Fourteen bowls.

Fourteen pieces of bread.

Pork stew with apples and onions.

No ceremony.

The kitchen workers ate too, standing or sitting on overturned baskets.

The tray woman sat on a step and removed one shoe.

Pell sat beside her.

She looked at him.

"Wall."

He moved six inches away from the passage.

She nodded.

We ate.

Marek finished first.

"One silver two," he said.

Rinna pointed her spoon at him.

"No."

"I was only appreciating."

"Appreciate your stew."

He did.

Davin had come in from the yard for food. He ate fast and left before
most of us finished.

"Horses," he said.

That was his evening.

Nessa talked with one of the kitchen women about soap.

Serra disappeared before dessert, if there was dessert.

Orin stayed and ate two bowls.

Iven was arguing quietly with Pell about whether the wooden fish counted
as company property if Pell had repaired more of it than remained
original.

The world had magic in it.

I had known that.

I had spent weeks thinking about magic until Hessa had made me stop
thinking about it unsupervised.

Then the road had filled up with wages, wheels, rooms, mud, onions, bad
stages, good actors, letters, horses, and people who needed me to move.

A woman had just used a little prepared silver clasp to make music
arrive from the wrong part of a room.

Nobody had gasped.

Nobody had called a Guild warder.

Harel had told her when to stop playing.

That interested me almost more than the clasp.

Almost.

I finished my stew.

Outside, the old center had gone dark except for lamps around the square
and Founder Hall.

We walked back to the wagons.

Rinna had paid the cooper yard through morning.

No rooms.

No loft.

Flat ground, water, wagons, horses.

Good enough.

Teren sat on the wagon tongue.

"Tomorrow," he said.

Marek groaned.

"What?"

"West."

I stopped.

Rinna looked at him.

"Carrow?"

"Eventually."

That word had changed since we left.

Teren continued, "Southwest road gets us back toward it. Two towns
between if we want work. One if we don't."

Rinna said, "Do we?"

"Want work?"

"Yes."

Teren looked at the wagons.

"Ask me tomorrow."

Davin came out of the dark.

"Rain."

"Tomorrow?"

"Maybe."

Marek pointed at me.

"His job."

I said, "I'm very good at maybe."

Nobody laughed because they had heard it before.

Fair.

I looked toward the old wall.

Blue shutters were somewhere beyond it.

Varo.

Throw clasp.

Prepared work.

Not much mana.

I could go in the morning.

I could look.

Hessa had not forbidden looking.

I knew exactly how dangerous that sentence was.

So I did not say it aloud.

For the first time since leaving Carrow, west was part of the route
again.

So was magic.

Neither had arrived dramatically.

They were simply there when I looked.

# CHAPTER 172

## THE CUSTOMER

The cooper was heating a barrel hoop when I woke.

Not in a forge.

The iron ring lay on three bricks in the yard. He touched a blackened
copper tab to it, said something I could not hear, and a dull red line
traveled around the hoop.

He watched it.

When the color reached the other side, he picked the hoop up with tongs
and carried it into the shed.

Nobody applauded.

Davin was already awake.

"Magic," I said.

"Hoop," he said.

"Both."

He looked at me.

"Move."

I moved.

The company was packing around me.

Rellin had gone gray with early morning. The old wall held the last of
the night in its cracks. Beyond it, chimney smoke had started rising. A
cart of apples rattled through the gate. Somewhere farther down the
road, a bell rang twice and then stopped.

Pell was rolling the mounting cloth.

"Do we own magic?" I asked.

He looked up.

"What?"

"For shows."

"Yes."

Nessa, kneeling beside the costume chest, said, "No."

Pell frowned.

"We do."

"We own prepared effects."

"That's magic."

"Not the way he means."

"I don't know how he means."

Neither did I.

I said, "The throw clasp."

Nessa closed the chest.

"What about it?"

"Do we have one?"

"No."

"Anything like it?"

"Not like it."

Pell said, "We have the blue lamp piece."

Nessa looked at him.

"What?"

"The blue lamp piece."

"That's not a throw."

"I didn't say it was."

"What does it do?" I asked.

Pell stood.

"Blue."

I waited.

"That's it?"

"It makes a lamp blue."

Nessa said, "It makes one lamp look colder from the house."

"Magic?"

"Prepared glass and a little cue."

"Who cues it?"

"Usually Davin."

From beside the wagon, Davin said, "No."

Nessa raised her voice.

"Who cued it last?"

"Rinna."

Rinna, counting food at the other wagon, said, "Once."

Pell pointed at me.

"See?"

I had seen the blue lamp.

I remembered it.

I had thought it was blue glass.

Apparently it was blue glass.

And magic.

"How much mana?"

Nessa stood.

"Very little."

"How little?"

"Greg."

"What?"

"We are leaving."

That was fair.

I found Teren near the horses.

"When?"

"Forty minutes."

"I want twenty."

"For what?"

"Instrument shop."

He looked at me.

"Why?"

"Throw clasp."

That got a different look.

Not surprise.

Recognition.

"You're buying one?"

"I don't know."

"Then don't."

"Useful."

"They're expensive."

"How expensive?"

"That's what shops are for."

I waited.

He sighed.

"Twenty minutes."

"Thirty?"

"Twenty."

"I have crutches."

"You had them when you asked."

Rinna said, "Take Pell."

Pell looked delighted.

Nessa said, "No."

Rinna looked at her.

Nessa looked at Pell.

"Bring him back."

"I was planning to."

"I wasn't talking to you."

Pell grinned.

We went.

The blue shutters were easy to find once we reached the square.

The shop was not.

The shutters belonged to two narrow windows over a doorway so dark I
thought the place was closed.

Pell walked in.

A little brass bell rang.

Then rang again from somewhere behind us.

I stopped.

Pell did not.

Inside smelled like wood, varnish, metal, and old dust.

Instruments hung from the walls. Some complete. Some not. A fiddle body
without a neck. Three drums stacked under a bench. Reeds in narrow
boxes. Strings looped over pegs. Brass fittings filled shallow trays.

A man sat at a workbench with his back to us.

"Varo?"

"No."

He did not turn.

"Do you know Varo?"

"No."

Pell looked at me.

The man said, "She's upstairs."

"Ah."

He turned then.

He was younger than I expected. Maybe thirty. Maybe younger. There was
silver dust on one sleeve.

"What?"

"Throw clasp."

"Buy?"

"Look."

"No."

Pell laughed.

I said, "Maybe buy."

"Then look."

He pointed to a glass-fronted cabinet.

There were six silver clips inside.

They did not look magical.

That annoyed me.

One was plain. One had two tiny loops worked into the side. One was
blackened at the tips. Two were mounted on little wooden blocks. The
last was larger and shaped to fit around something round.

"Which is throw?"

"Four."

"Which four?"

"The four."

Pell leaned closer.

"That's a reed seat."

The man nodded.

"Good."

I had no idea which one Pell meant.

A woman came down the stairs carrying a bundle of thin wooden strips.

"Why is an actor touching my cabinet?"

I was not touching it.

I looked at my hands anyway.

The younger man said, "He's looking."

The woman put the strips on the bench.

"Actors look with fingers."

"I'm not."

"Yet."

"Varo?"

"Unfortunately."

She looked at Pell.

"You're too young to buy anything."

"I'm with him."

"That makes it worse."

I liked her.

I said, "I saw a throw clasp last night. Lap strings. Founder Hall."

"Yessa's."

"I didn't get her name."

"You got mine."

"Yes."

"What do you want it to do?"

That was exactly the wrong question.

"Move sound."

Varo stared at me.

Pell said, "He means throw."

"I know what he means. He doesn't."

I said, "Make the sound come from somewhere else."

"How far?"

"I don't know."

"Which direction?"

"I don't know."

"What room?"

"I don't know."

"What instrument?"

"I don't have one."

Varo looked at Pell.

"Is he always like this?"

Pell said, "More now."

"Good. Means he's learning."

I almost smiled.

Then Varo added, "Slowly."

She opened the cabinet.

"Yessa's clasp is built for her board. You put it on a fiddle, it does
badly. You put it on a voice, it does nothing. You put it in a street
and ask it to throw through six carts, you wasted money."

She took out the plainest clip.

"Prepared channel. Maker sets the bias. Player gives it a cue. Tiny draw
if the preparation is good."

"What if the player can't draw?"

"Then buy a charged one."

I looked at her.

"Charged?"

"Costs more. Lasts less."

"How much?"

"For you?"

"Why for me?"

"You ask expensive questions."

Pell covered his mouth.

Varo said, "Basic fitted throw, one silver six. Better one, more.
Charged, depends. Custom, don't bother."

One silver six.

I stopped wanting to touch it.

"That's more than I have."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"You won't buy the wrong one."

She put it back.

I looked at the cabinet again.

"What is it changing?"

"Sound."

"Yes, but the sound itself or where people think it is?"

Varo paused.

Not long.

Long enough.

"Where did you get that?"

"Yessa said those aren't always different."

"Yessa says things when she doesn't want to explain."

"Do you?"

"Constantly."

Pell was looking at a small brass disk on the counter.

Varo slapped his hand away without looking.

"That's hot."

"It isn't."

"It was yesterday."

Pell withdrew his hand.

I said, "So?"

Varo leaned against the bench.

"A throw doesn't make a second sound. It doesn't pick up a note and
carry it across a room like a bucket. It changes the path enough that
your ear lies to you."

"My ear?"

"Your head. Your ear is trying."

"That's illusion."

"Sometimes."

"What other time is it?"

"Acoustics."

That was not satisfying.

Varo did not care.

She picked up one of the wooden strips and checked its edge against the
light.

"You actors always want magic to be the interesting part."

Pell said, "I'm crew."

"You people are worse."

I said, "How much is the magic?"

"In what?"

"The effect."

Varo looked at me again.

"Wrong question."

"Why?"

"Because if the room is wrong, more magic gives you expensive wrong."

That sounded like Hessa.

Not the words.

The refusal.

I frowned.

Varo frowned back.

"See? Now we're both unhappy."

Pell said, "Show him the bell."

"No."

"Bell?"

"No."

The brass bell over the door rang.

Then the sound came from behind me again.

I turned.

Varo had not moved.

The younger man was smiling.

"Bell," Pell said.

I looked up.

The bell was ordinary brass.

A tiny black strip had been fixed to the inside of the door frame.

"Throw?"

"Cheap one," Varo said.

"How cheap?"

"Not for sale."

"Why?"

"It lies badly."

"It worked."

"You turned around."

"Exactly."

"You're standing three feet from it and weren't expecting it. Put twenty
people in here twice and half of them point at the door."

That was interesting.

"Shortcut," Pell said.

Varo nodded.

"The room does most of it."

I looked at the narrow shop.

Hard walls. Low ceiling. Shelves. Hanging instruments.

"You put the false sound where the room already makes sense."

Varo said, "Sometimes."

"So you need less."

"Sometimes."

"Could you do that with a voice?"

"Yes."

"An actor?"

"Yes."

"Onstage?"

"Yes."

"Offstage?"

"Obviously."

Pell said, "We do."

I looked at him.

"What?"

"We do."

"When?"

"Ghost piece."

"I haven't seen the ghost piece."

"You weren't in it."

"Who throws?"

"Nobody."

I waited.

Pell grinned.

"Tube."

Varo laughed.

I said, "Tube."

"Under the floor if we have one. Behind cloth if we don't. Little metal
mouth. Actor speaks into the other end."

"That's not magic."

"Correct."

"Then why did you say we do?"

"Because it sounds like throw."

Varo pointed at him.

"Keep that one."

Pell looked pleased.

I was annoyed again.

Not at him.

At the answer.

A tube could do what I had spent the last ten minutes asking magic to
do.

Not everywhere.

Not as cleanly.

But enough, in the right place.

Varo picked up another fitting.

"Most stage work is cheating."

Pell said, "Craft."

"Same thing if you're paid."

I said, "What about a veil?"

Varo's expression changed.

"Why?"

"Nessa said throw isn't veil."

"Nessa's right."

"What does veil do?"

"Ask Nessa."

"You're the shop."

"I'm the instrument shop."

That was fair too.

She held up the fitting.

"This keeps a reed from splitting when somebody cues badly. You want
stage veils, find a stage maker."

"Where?"

"Not in Rellin."

"Carrow?"

"Probably."

"Probably?"

"I don't live there."

I thought of East Market Hall.

Of ropes.

Paint.

Lamps.

Things I had stopped seeing because I knew where they were stored.

"What do theatres use?"

"Whatever works."

"Magic."

"Sometimes."

"Mechanisms."

"Usually."

"Both."

"Best when nobody can tell."

That stayed.

Not because it was profound.

Because she said it while scraping varnish from a brass fitting with her
thumbnail.

I looked at the cabinet.

One silver six.

No.

"Do you have anything inert?"

Varo said, "Everything is inert if you don't use it."

"I mean something prepared but not active."

"Why?"

"I can't draw unsupervised."

The shop changed.

Only slightly.

The younger man stopped smiling.

Varo put the fitting down.

"Guild?"

"Restricted."

"Then don't buy a clasp."

"I wasn't going to activate it."

"People who say that in shops activate things."

"I don't."

"Good."

She opened a drawer and took out a narrow piece of silver-colored metal.

Not a clasp.

A failed clasp, maybe. Flat on one end, bent on the other.

"This was cut wrong."

"What does it do?"

"Nothing."

"Prepared?"

"Started."

"Meaning?"

"Channel was marked. Bias wasn't set. Scrap."

"How much?"

"One copper."

Pell said, "That's garbage."

Varo said, "Yes."

I bought it.

Pell stared at me.

"She said garbage."

"I heard."

Varo took my copper.

"No activation."

"It can't activate."

"No filing."

"Why?"

"You'll ruin the mark."

"It's garbage."

"It's educational garbage."

Pell made a sound.

I put the piece into my pocket.

Not with the clasp for Lyssa.

Different pocket.

"Can Hessa look at it?"

Varo shrugged.

"I don't know Hessa."

"She's Guild."

"Then she can frown at it professionally."

That sounded possible.

We left.

Outside, Pell said, "You paid for broken metal."

"Yes."

"I could have found you broken metal."

"Prepared broken metal."

"Still broken."

"Educational."

"Garbage."

"You're young."

"I'm right."

He was.

We reached the wagons late.

Not very late.

Late enough.

Teren looked at me.

"Twenty minutes."

"Shop was educational."

"Did you buy garbage?"

Pell said, "Yes."

Teren closed his eyes.

Nessa said, "What?"

I showed her the scrap.

She took it.

Turned it over.

Looked at the faint marks.

"Throw blank."

"Failed."

"Obviously."

"Varo said the channel was marked but the bias wasn't set."

Nessa handed it back.

"Then it's useless."

"For doing it."

"Yes."

"What about looking?"

She frowned.

Not like Hessa.

More efficiently.

Then she reached into the prop chest.

I expected blue glass.

Instead she pulled out a small wooden mouthpiece attached to six feet of
narrow leather tube.

"Ghost."

Pell looked triumphant.

Nessa said, "This is what you learn first."

I held it.

"Tube."

"Tube."

"No magic."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because it works."

She took it back.

Then she lifted a little square of smoky glass wrapped in cloth.

"Blue lamp."

The glass had a thin pale line worked around one edge.

"Prepared?"

"Yes."

"Who made it?"

"No idea."

"How does it work?"

"Rinna touches the cue mark after the lamp is lit."

"Mana?"

"Small."

"Could I?"

"No."

That answer came quickly.

I nodded.

Nessa wrapped it again.

"But you can hang it."

"What?"

"You can learn where it goes."

That was different.

She pointed toward the rear wagon.

"After we stop."

Teren said, "We are stopping now."

Nessa looked at him.

"Later."

"Good."

We left Rellin.

The southwest road dropped out of orchard country in long shallow turns.

For the first mile, barrels passed us going the other way.

Then fewer.

Then none.

The land opened.

Low stone walls continued between fields, but the orchards thinned into
pasture and grain.

At a roadside shrine, a little glass bead burned with steady amber light
beneath a stone roof.

No candle.

No smoke.

Marek did not look at it.

Serra did not look at it.

I did.

Then I nearly stepped into a rut.

Davin said, "Road."

I watched the road.

At midday we stopped beside a stream.

Rinna gave us bread and the last of the supper cheese.

Marek complained there was no hot food.

Nobody answered.

He ate.

Serra sat twenty yards away under a tree reading something.

Orin had gone upstream.

Pell was throwing pebbles into the water and trying to hit the same
patch twice.

Nessa sat beside the prop chest.

I sat near her.

She looked at me.

"Lamp?"

"Yes."

She sighed.

"Get it."

I did.

The blue lamp piece was smaller in daylight.

Less impressive.

Just smoky glass with a pale worked line around it.

Nessa made me hold it by the cloth.

"Why?"

"Oil."

"From my hand?"

"Yes."

"Does that matter?"

"Eventually."

She showed me the hook.

Not the magic.

The hook.

How the glass sat in front of the lamp without touching the hot chimney.
How the angle mattered. How it looked from the front. How it looked from
the side.

"If they see the edge, it's bad," she said.

"Because they see the magic?"

"Because they see glass."

"Oh."

"If the cue works perfectly and they see a square of glass hanging in
front of the lamp, you've made blue glass."

"Which it is."

"Exactly."

She had me hang it from a wagon lantern that was not lit.

I did it wrong.

She moved it half an inch.

The edge disappeared behind the lamp frame.

"Again."

I did it again.

Wrong differently.

Pell came over.

"He's bad."

"Go away."

He stayed.

Third time, I got it.

Nessa nodded.

"Fine."

"Now cue?"

"No."

"I know."

"Good."

She took the glass off.

I said, "How much of the effect is the cue?"

"Small."

"How much is the glass?"

"Some."

"How much is where you hang it?"

"Enough."

"How much is the audience not looking at the lamp?"

Nessa looked at me.

Pell stopped throwing stones.

"More," she said.

That was all.

She wrapped the glass.

I took the failed throw blank out of my pocket.

Nessa looked at it.

"Hessa will hate that."

"Why?"

"Because you bought it."

"She might not."

"She'll frown."

"Probably."

"What are you asking her?"

I looked at the scrap.

I had been asking myself that since the shop.

Not how to make a throw.

Hessa did not know stagecraft. Or if she did, she had never shown any
interest in teaching me.

That wasn't her job.

The troupe knew how to make an audience look away from a lamp.

Varo knew how to make an ear lie.

Hessa knew what happened when I drew mana and failed to make anything
outside myself do what I wanted.

Those were not the same problem.

Maybe they touched.

"I don't know yet."

Nessa took the lamp back.

"Good."

We packed.

By afternoon, clouds had gathered behind us.

Davin noticed first.

Of course.

We kept moving.

Teren rode on the front wagon for a while, then walked.

At a fork, he stopped to read a weather-darkened board.

One road went west.

One southwest.

"Which?" Marek asked.

Teren looked at Rinna.

Rinna looked at Davin.

Davin looked at the sky.

"Southwest."

"Work?" I asked.

Teren said, "Town tomorrow."

"Show?"

"Maybe."

Marek groaned.

I said nothing.

The southwest road still bent west.

Carrow was no longer behind everything.

It was somewhere ahead of some of it.

I touched my coat.

The brass clasp for Lyssa was still there.

In my other pocket, the failed throw blank clicked against two copper.

I moved it so it would not scratch them.

We walked.

At the next rise, I could see the road for a long way.

Fields.

A stand of dark trees.

Two wagons ahead of us.

A little village farther off, its lamps beginning to come on one by one.

One lamp brightened green before settling to yellow.

Nobody stopped.

Neither did we.

I had spent one copper on something that could not do magic.

I had learned how to hang blue glass.

Somehow I had more questions than before.

That felt promising.

Also expensive.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 173

## THE LAMPLIGHTER

The next town had a sign that lied less than most actors.

**HALVER. COACHES. BEDS. HORSES. HOT FOOD.**

Below that, in smaller paint:

**PLAYERS ASK FIRST.**

Marek read it twice.

"I feel specifically attacked."

Teren said, "Good."

We came down into Halver before noon.

It sat where three roads met around a shallow river, with a stone bridge
on the west side and a newer timber bridge to the south. Most of the
town seemed built for people who intended to leave it. Inns. Stables.
Wheelwrights. Two smithies. A long coach yard with six bays and a roofed
gallery. Shops selling food that could survive pockets.

A green-glass road marker stood at the first fork. The lettering
brightened as our wagon shadow passed over it.

WEST BRIDGE: CARROW ROAD.

I stopped looking long enough that Pell walked into me.

"Move."

"Carrow."

"I can read."

"Can you?"

"Better than you."

He went around me.

Carrow road.

Not Carrow.

But the road that went there.

That was new.

Davin took the wagons toward the coach yard. Teren and Rinna went inside
the largest inn. Nessa disappeared into a lamp seller. Serra said she
needed soap and left before anyone asked why. Orin was simply gone.

Marek looked at the hot-food sign.

"I am going to become a customer."

"You have money?"

"Some."

"Personal expenditure?"

"Do not ruin this."

He left.

I stayed with Davin.

"Rear," he said.

I went to the rear wagon.

Nothing happened.

A coach came in.

I moved a bucket.

A stable boy shouted at another stable boy.

Davin crawled under the axle.

I watched the lane.

This was apparently my life now.

Five minutes later Teren came back.

"Show."

"Here?"

"Maybe."

"That's not show."

"Six o'clock. Coach gallery. Inn wants twenty-five minutes before supper
traffic."

"Pay?"

"Fifteen copper company. Two pitchers small beer. No food."

"That's bad."

Rinna came out behind him.

"It's acceptable."

"Then good."

"Don't help."

Teren pointed at the gallery.

"Shopkeeper. Widow. Short King if room holds."

"Sword?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Coaches."

That was fair.

Nessa returned carrying lamp oil and a paper twist of wicks.

She looked at the gallery.

Then at the light.

Then at Teren.

"Blue?"

Teren said, "Maybe."

I said, "I can hang it."

Nessa looked at me.

Pell appeared from nowhere.

"He can."

"Quiet."

"He did it three times."

"One time."

"Three attempts."

Nessa handed me the oil.

"Carry."

I carried.

The coach gallery was long and narrow, built over the stable offices on
one side of the yard. The open rail faced the coaches below. Behind it
ran a wall with three doors, one staircase, and hooks for travelers'
coats. Benches could be turned toward either the yard or the wall.

The innkeeper, a woman named Fera, wanted us against the far wall.

Teren wanted the stair end.

Nessa wanted neither.

"That lamp," she said.

There was a wall lamp halfway down the gallery.

Fera said, "What about it?"

"Can we use it?"

"You can light it."

"Can we hang glass on it?"

"What glass?"

Nessa showed her the smoky square.

Fera held out her hand.

Nessa did not give it to her.

"Prepared?"

"Yes."

"Heat?"

"No."

"Smoke?"

"No."

"Stain?"

"No."

Fera looked at Rinna.

"If it stains my wall, two copper."

"It won't."

"If it does."

"One."

"Two."

Rinna said, "Fine."

Fera nodded.

That was the magical safety inspection.

I had expected more.

Nessa pointed at the lamp.

"Hang it."

I did.

Wrong.

Not badly.

Just enough that she clicked her tongue.

"What?"

"Gallery rail."

I stepped back.

From where the audience would sit, the pale edge of the glass caught
daylight from the open side.

I moved it.

"Too far."

I moved it back.

"Stop touching it like it insulted you."

"It did."

Pell leaned over the rail.

"Still see the bottom."

I adjusted the hook.

The edge disappeared behind the iron lamp frame.

Nessa walked three benches down.

"Fine."

I smiled.

"Don't."

"I didn't."

"You did."

Fera said, "What does it do?"

Nessa said, "Blue."

Fera waited.

"That's all?"

"That's enough."

I looked at the wall.

The lamp was not lit.

The glass did nothing.

A coach rolled into the yard below us. Six passengers got out. One
argued immediately about a trunk.

Fera watched them.

"You're not blocking that stair."

Teren said, "We won't."

"You are."

We were.

She made us move two benches and the prop basket.

Ten minutes later three passengers came up the stair exactly where the
basket had been.

Local people knew where the future happened.

I was getting used to that.

By afternoon the gallery smelled of lamp oil, horse, beer, and wet wool.

A light rain had started. Not enough to stop coaches. Enough to make
everyone who arrived want shelter.

That helped.

Teren changed the bill.

"King first."

Marek said, "Correct."

"Short."

"Incorrect."

"Widow. Shopkeeper."

"Why King first?"

"People are arriving."

"I can hold them."

"No. You can be loud while they sit down."

Marek considered that.

"Also correct."

The blue lamp was for Widow.

I was not in Widow.

That meant I had a job.

Nessa showed me the ordinary lamp beside it.

"At the turn, Pell shutters this."

Pell touched the shutter.

"Then Rinna cues blue."

Rinna was below arguing with Fera about where the collection bowl could
go.

I said, "What do I do?"

"Nothing."

"I hung it."

"Yes."

"So I'm done."

"Until it slips."

"Does it slip?"

"If you hang it badly."

I looked at the hook.

Nessa walked away.

I looked at the hook harder.

The failed throw blank was in my pocket.

I had taken it out twice on the road that morning.

Not to do anything.

Just to look at the marks.

They were faint and irritating. A shallow line split near the middle,
curved toward the bent end, then stopped. I could not tell whether the
split mattered or whether it was where Varo had decided the piece was
already ruined.

I had tried comparing it to Hessa's diagrams in memory.

That had been useless.

Hessa drew mana.

Varo marked metal.

Nessa hid glass.

Pell used a tube.

All of them could make something happen outside the body.

Only one of those things was the problem Hessa and I had actually been
testing.

I put the blank away.

Marek was practicing nothing.

He stood at the far end of the gallery wearing half his King coat while
eating a meat pie.

"Preparation," he said.

"Food."

"Both."

"Growth."

"Fuck you."

He had bought the pie himself.

I was proud of him.

I did not tell him.

By six, the gallery had thirty people in it.

Then forty.

Some were travelers waiting for coaches. Some were staying at the inn.
Some were locals who had heard there were players. A group of carters
stood along the open rail because they did not want to pay for drinks.

Nobody had paid to see us.

Fera had.

That changed the room.

Teren stood near the stair and watched people settle.

A coach horn sounded outside.

He waited.

The coach came in.

Passengers climbed the stairs.

He waited.

Fera looked at him.

He held up one finger.

A serving girl crossed with six bowls.

Then Teren nodded to Marek.

Marek walked into the middle of the gallery and said, "I have inherited
a kingdom."

A carter said, "Sorry."

Marek looked at him.

"So am I."

The room turned.

Not all at once.

Enough.

The King piece was short.

Marek was good.

That still annoyed me sometimes.

He could take a room that was not interested and make his annoyance seem
like their fault.

Iven joined him.

They did the debt section.

A coachman came up the stairs during it.

Marek moved half a step without looking.

The coachman passed behind him.

No collision.

No pause.

No lesson.

Just work.

The piece ended.

Some people clapped.

A child near the rail asked whether Marek was really a king.

Marek said, "Temporarily."

That got more laughter than the ending.

Widow came next.

Serra entered in dark cloth.

Orin sat on a bench with his head down.

The first part of the piece was ordinary light.

Warm wall lamps.

Rain outside.

People shifting.

A cup dropped downstairs.

Then Serra said, "You left the room warm."

Pell closed the shutter on the ordinary lamp.

Not dark.

Less warm.

Rinna touched the cue mark.

I did not see mana.

I was not looking for it.

The smoky glass changed.

Barely.

The lamp behind it cooled from yellow toward a thin blue-white.

Serra's face changed with it.

Not shape.

Not color exactly.

The shadows under her eyes deepened. The dark cloth stopped looking
brown and became almost black.

Orin lifted his head.

Behind him, Pell pulled a gray cloth away from the wall.

That was all.

A gray cloth.

It revealed pale stone.

The audience went quiet.

I knew the wall was real.

I knew the blue was a prepared glass.

I knew Pell had hidden the pale stone with cloth before the show.

I knew Serra had turned her body so the colder lamp took one side of her
face.

I knew Orin had waited until the room changed before looking up.

The room knew none of that separately.

It knew the room had become colder.

It had not.

That was the strange part.

The rain was real.

The pale stone was real.

Serra's face was real.

The shadow was real.

The lamp was really bluer.

Nothing in front of them needed to be false.

The cold was.

A woman pulled her shawl tighter.

I stared at her.

Nessa hit my arm.

"Hook."

The glass had shifted.

Almost nothing.

One corner had slipped forward.

I reached up and steadied the frame.

Not the prepared line.

The frame.

The edge disappeared again.

The woman kept watching Serra.

Nobody watched me.

That mattered more than I wanted it to.

Widow ended with Serra turning away from Orin.

Pell opened the ordinary lamp shutter.

Rinna released the cue.

Warm yellow returned.

People moved again.

Someone breathed loudly.

A man near the stair said, "Fuck."

Fera smiled.

Not at us.

At the room.

Then she went downstairs because someone was shouting about a horse.

Teren pointed at me.

Shopkeeper.

I had about twelve seconds.

I had been watching the lamp.

I had not put on my coat.

"Fuck."

Pell threw it at me.

I caught one sleeve.

The other folded under.

I went out wearing it wrong.

Iven saw.

His mouth twitched.

I said, "You owe me money."

He said, "You appear to owe your tailor."

The room laughed.

I looked down.

One side of my coat was tucked under my arm.

"Separate account."

More laughter.

Good.

Then I forgot the next line.

Not all of it.

The first three words.

Iven waited.

I could hear the rain.

I could hear somebody downstairs dragging something heavy.

I said, "You have delayed payment."

Wrong line.

Right information.

Iven answered.

We continued.

The scene did not die.

I stopped trying to find the missing words.

The Shopkeeper wanted money.

Iven did not have it.

That was true enough.

Halfway through, a man at the rail said, "Take his boots."

I said, "I have standards."

The man looked at my peg.

I saw him decide whether to say something.

He did not.

Iven said, "Do you?"

I said, "No."

That got him.

He laughed.

Actually laughed.

Then had to turn it into a cough.

The audience saw that too.

We finished.

Teren cut the last planned exchange because another coach horn sounded.

We were off before the passengers came up.

Twenty-three minutes.

Close enough.

Fera paid Rinna fifteen copper.

No argument.

She also sent up the two pitchers.

Marek had already acquired a cup.

Rinna slapped his hand.

"Company."

"I am company."

"Later."

Fera looked at the blue lamp.

"Do that every time?"

Nessa said, "No."

"Why not?"

"Wrong room."

Fera looked around her own gallery.

"What makes this right?"

Nessa pointed at the open rail.

"Rain."

Fera looked at the rain.

Then at the pale stone wall.

Then at Serra.

"Huh."

She went downstairs.

I followed Nessa to the lamp.

"Was the rain important?"

"Yes."

"You didn't make the rain."

"No."

"The stone?"

"Wall."

"Serra's face?"

"Serra."

"The cloth?"

"Pell."

"The blue?"

"Glass."

"And people felt cold."

Nessa looked at me.

"Did you?"

"No."

She waited.

"Maybe."

"Then stop talking."

She took the glass down.

I said, "Nothing was fake."

Pell, carrying the gray cloth, said, "I'm fake."

Nessa said, "You're unpaid if you tear that."

He folded it.

I stood there.

Nothing was fake.

That was not exactly true.

The room had lied.

No.

We had.

No.

We had shown them things that were true and let them make the wrong
thing out of it.

Rain.

Stone.

Blue light.

A widow saying the room had been warm.

A woman tightening her shawl because she already knew rain meant cold.

The effect had not needed to create cold.

It had needed the room to remember cold.

"Greg."

Teren.

I turned.

"Bowls."

"What?"

"Take them down."

There were empty cups and two bowls on the bench.

I took them down.

That was probably healthier.

The kitchen had a flat iron plate with a small red mark worked into one
corner. A cook set a pot on it, touched the mark, and went back to
cutting onions.

The pot began steaming.

I watched for two seconds.

The cook said, "Move."

I moved.

Outside, the rain had thickened.

Davin had put canvas over the wagon loads.

The long box was under it with everything else.

Dry.

Upright.

Uninteresting.

Good.

Rinna found me near the stable.

"Two copper."

She handed me two.

"Show?"

"Rellin."

"Oh."

"Your share."

I looked at the coins.

"Now?"

"Unless you want me to keep them."

"No."

"Then now."

"How much did Marek get?"

"Ask Marek."

"Serra?"

"Greg."

"Fine."

She left.

I put the two copper away.

The failed throw blank clicked against them.

Wrong pocket again.

I moved it.

Marek came out carrying a bowl.

"Hot food."

"Did you buy that?"

"No."

"Steal it?"

"Relationship."

"With who?"

"The cook."

"What's her name?"

He looked at the bowl.

"Soup."

"Strong relationship."

He ate.

We slept in the coach yard for three copper company, wagons and horses
included, no rooms.

The rain stopped sometime after midnight.

In the morning the town smelled washed and metallic.

Davin had us moving early.

Fera sold Rinna bread.

Nessa bought another wick.

Serra returned from somewhere with soap that smelled like pine.

Orin was already at the wagon when I woke.

I did not ask.

At the west fork, the green road marker was dull in daylight.

The letters still said:

CARROW ROAD.

Teren stood beside it.

"One town if we go straight," he said.

Rinna asked, "Work?"

"Maybe."

She looked at him.

He smiled.

She did not.

"Two days?" I asked.

Davin said, "If road."

Everyone looked at him.

He looked back.

"Road."

Marek groaned.

I looked west.

Two days if road.

Maybe three.

Maybe work.

Maybe not.

Lyssa was somewhere at the other end of that direction.

Hessa too.

I touched the failed throw blank through my pocket.

I knew what I wanted to ask Hessa now.

Not how to make a room cold.

We had not made the room cold.

I wanted to know how little had to be real before the rest of it became
true to somebody watching.

That was probably not the right question.

Hessa would frown.

Good.

I had time to make it worse.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 174

## THE RETURNER

We did not perform in the next town.

Teren tried.

That was different.

By noon we had reached a place called Brant, which had one stone bridge,
two inns, a tannery, a smith, and a square too small to deserve the
word. Teren went into the larger inn. Rinna went into the smaller one.
Marek found a woman selling meat pies.

The rest of us waited beside the wagons.

Ten minutes later Teren came out.

"No."

Rinna came out across the square.

"No."

Marek came back with a pie.

"Yes."

Teren looked at him.

"What?"

"Different negotiation."

We kept moving.

That should not have surprised me.

It did.

For most of the trip, every place had become work if we waited long
enough, asked enough people, accepted enough mud, or stood beside enough
cheese.

Brant did not want us.

A man was repairing the bridge rail with a stone-setting tool. It looked
like a short iron mallet with a pale mark down the handle. He tapped
mortar between two stones, touched the mark with his thumb, and the wet
seam tightened darker around the edge.

He did not want us either.

The road west left town between the tannery and a field full of geese.

Pell said, "We could have done the goose piece."

"We don't have a goose piece," I said.

"We could."

"With what goose?"

He pointed at the field.

"That goose."

One of the geese charged the fence.

I said, "No."

Pell laughed.

"What?"

"Real goose."

"So?"

"Bad actor."

"Good goose."

"Exactly."

Nessa, walking ahead of us, said, "Don't steal livestock."

"I wasn't."

Pell said, "He was casting."

"I was not casting."

"Different casting."

I hated him.

The goose followed us along the fence until the road bent away.

For the next hour I thought about the goose more than I should have.

Not magically.

Practically.

If we wanted a goose onstage, a real goose would be the most truthful
possible goose.

It would also shit where it wanted, leave when it wanted, bite Marek,
and refuse every entrance.

A wooden goose would be false and better.

Unless the point was the sound.

Then maybe you did not need a goose at all.

I stopped there.

Mostly because Davin said, "Rear."

I went to the rear wagon.

He had heard something in the left wheel.

I had not.

He crouched beside it while I watched the road.

A freight wagon approached from behind. I moved our water bucket, then
the small prop basket Pell had left too near the wheel.

Davin spun the wheel a fraction.

"Again," I said.

He looked at me.

"What?"

"The sound."

"I know."

Right.

He was not asking me.

I watched the lane.

The freight wagon passed.

Its driver lifted two fingers.

I did the same.

Davin tightened something I could not see.

"Done."

We walked.

By late afternoon, the road had widened enough for two wagons to pass
without negotiation. Old mile stones appeared at intervals. Most were
worn nearly blank.

One still had enough letters.

CARROW 19.

I stopped.

Marek nearly hit me.

"Again?"

"Nineteen."

"I can count."

"Can you?"

"Fuck off."

Nineteen miles was not two days.

Not really.

Not if the road held.

Davin looked at the stone.

"Tomorrow."

Teren said, "Tomorrow."

That moved through me strangely.

Not excitement exactly.

Something less useful.

I checked my coat.

The brass clasp was there.

The failed throw blank was in my trouser pocket.

I checked that too.

Pell saw.

"Still garbage?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"If it became expensive while you walked, I'd be worried."

We camped that night at a road house six miles past Brant.

Not an inn.

A road house.

The distinction was apparently that an inn had rooms and a road house
had walls you could stand near while paying for everything separately.

The yard cost two copper for both wagons.

Water was free.

Hay was not.

Hot stew was three copper a bowl, which meant none of us bought it
except Marek.

He stood beside the cook fire holding his bowl.

"Personal expenditure."

"You already used that."

"It remains accurate."

Rinna bought bread and a pot of beans for the company.

We ate under a lean-to while rain threatened and failed to happen.

A courier stopped after dark.

His satchel had a waxed flap with a narrow prepared seal stitched into
the leather. When he closed it, the line flashed once and went dull.

I watched.

He noticed.

"Courier seal. I only use it."

"How does it know it's closed?"

"It doesn't."

"What does it know?"

"I don't know. I carry letters."

That was interesting.

"What does it know?"

He stared at me.

"I don't know. I carry letters."

Then he went inside.

That was probably healthier too.

Serra laughed into her bread.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You laughed."

"I did."

"At me."

"Probably."

She ate.

Across the yard, Pell and Nessa were repairing the hem of Marek's King
coat. Orin sat on an overturned bucket talking quietly with the
road-house owner. Davin had disappeared into the stable. Teren and Rinna
were arguing about whether to leave before sunrise or merely at sunrise.

Nobody was discussing my questions.

I liked that.

I took the failed throw blank out.

Not to use it.

There was nothing to use.

The courier's seal had made me think about the marked line.

That was all.

The preparation marks were easier to see near the fire.

One line.

A branch.

A curve.

Stop.

I knew nothing.

That was becoming clearer.

I had spent weeks learning to draw mana under Hessa's supervision. I
could shape what I felt. I could repeat that much. We had tried to make
something outside me answer.

Three times.

Nothing we could establish.

Varo could mark a piece of metal so that, if she finished it correctly,
a tiny cue would make a sound seem to come from the wrong place.

The troupe could make a room feel cold with rain, stone, cloth, a lamp,
and a woman turning her face.

Pell could make a ghost with a tube.

A real goose was worse than a fake goose.

These did not fit together.

That was probably why I kept trying to fit them together.

Marek sat beside me with his stew.

"You look stupid."

"I'm thinking."

"Same."

"How much did that cost?"

"Do not make this about money."

"Three copper?"

He protected the bowl.

"Leave me."

I did.

Later, I checked the clasp again.

That was worse.

The little brass leaves were still wrapped.

I had bought them days ago.

Long enough that the purchase had stopped feeling like a decision and
started feeling like an object I was responsible for delivering.

I imagined giving it to Lyssa.

Then I imagined explaining why I had carried it halfway across the road
network instead of giving it to her immediately like a normal person.

Then I stopped imagining.

The road house had a loft.

We did not have the loft.

We had the yard.

I slept under the wagon.

In the morning, something screamed in the trees.

I woke hard enough to hit my shoulder on wood.

"What the fuck?"

Pell was already awake.

"Fox."

"That was not a fox."

"Fox."

"No."

Davin, somewhere near the horses, said, "Fox."

I lay back down.

It screamed again.

That was terrible.

I had heard foxes before.

Apparently not that fox.

Marek crawled out from a blanket.

"What died?"

"Nothing," Pell said.

"Then why is it making that sound?"

"Fox."

Marek stared toward the trees.

I said, "Good stage sound."

Pell looked at me.

"No."

"Why?"

"Too ugly."

"That's why."

Nessa threw a rolled stocking at him.

"Pack."

We packed.

The fox screamed once more while we were tying the rear cover.

I listened.

Not because I wanted to reproduce it.

Because I had been wrong about what a fox sounded like.

That felt relevant in a way I did not trust.

If somebody made that sound in a dark theatre and told me it was a woman
dying, I would believe them.

If they told me fox first, I would hear fox.

The sound did not change.

I did.

"Greg."

I looked up.

Rinna held out the Halver money.

"One."

"One what?"

"Copper."

"My share?"

"Yes."

"Only one?"

"You didn't eat company stew because there wasn't any."

"That doesn't seem related."

"It isn't."

I took the copper.

She moved on.

Pell got something too.

I did not count.

The road west was cold and clear.

No rain.

No fair traffic.

No market.

Just people moving.

A farmer with empty baskets.

Two women riding small horses.

A cart carrying glazed tiles.

A man walking six sheep and swearing at all of them equally.

At a low bridge, a prepared counter fixed to the toll post clicked once
for our first wagon and once for the second.

The keeper still looked outside and charged Rinna by hand.

I pointed at the counter.

"What does that do?"

"Counts."

"You count."

"Yes."

"Then why?"

"So I know if I counted."

That was the entire magical system.

I loved it.

We crossed.

Around midday the country began changing.

Not dramatically.

Fields became familiar in the way roads could become familiar before I
remembered why.

A ditch with white stones.

A stand of crooked trees.

A hill I had seen from the other direction.

Then a roadside shrine with one chipped corner.

I knew that shrine.

I stopped.

Serra looked back.

"You all right?"

"Yes."

She followed my eyes.

"Been here?"

"Yes."

She nodded.

Nothing else.

Carrow was no longer a direction.

It was around things I recognized.

We stopped for bread near a cluster of houses.

Teren did not ask for work.

That was when I knew we were actually going home.

Marek did ask whether there was hot food.

There was not.

He took it personally.

By midafternoon, the road grew busier.

Carrow traffic.

I knew that too.

Carts coming out with empty crates.

Workers going in.

A Guild wagon with the bronze mark painted on the side.

Two students in gray coats walking too slowly in the road.

A woman selling prepared lamp stones from a shoulder tray called prices
at passing carts.

Nobody cared that I had been gone.

Good.

Then the city appeared.

Not all of it.

First the outer roofs.

Then smoke.

Then the higher buildings.

Then the road widened.

I had expected something.

I did not know what.

Maybe for it to look smaller.

It did not.

Maybe for me to feel different.

I did.

That was less useful.

Teren called from ahead.

"Hall first."

Rinna said, "Wagons first."

Teren looked back.

"Hall after wagons."

Davin said, "Wagons."

The wagons won.

We entered Carrow through afternoon traffic.

A gate worker waved us through after looking at the company papers.

No recognition.

No problem.

A porter shouted at Marek to move.

Marek shouted back that he was moving.

He was not.

Serra disappeared at the first market turn.

Not metaphorically.

She said, "Later," and walked away.

Orin left two streets after that.

Pell asked where.

Nessa said, "Not your business."

Pell said, "I know."

He still watched Orin go.

I did too.

Then I saw East Market Hall at the end of the street.

That hit harder than the gate.

The building was exactly where we had left it.

Which was unreasonable.

I had crossed half the world.

Not actually.

Enough of it.

The hall had stayed still.

Davin took the wagons around back.

We unloaded.

Not everything.

Company things.

Costume chests.

Prop baskets.

The Sword board.

The long iron-cornered box.

Nobody opened it.

Two workers carried it inside with Davin directing them.

"Other side."

They turned.

"Up."

They lifted.

"Wall."

They put it against the wall.

That was all.

I carried the blue-lamp piece.

Nessa saw.

"Careful."

"I know."

"That's when people drop things."

I carried it more carefully.

Inside the hall smelled like dust, old wood, lamp oil, and somebody
else's lunch.

Home was too strong a word.

Familiar was not.

It was both.

Teren was already talking to someone about tomorrow.

Tomorrow.

Of course.

Rinna was counting something.

Pell had found the wooden fish and was making it bite a rope.

Marek had disappeared toward the kitchen.

I stood with my bag.

Nobody told me what to do.

That was rare enough that I waited.

Nessa walked past.

"Go."

"Where?"

She stopped.

"Wherever you've been trying to get back to."

"Oh."

"Bring your bag."

I looked down.

I still had it.

"Right."

Outside, Carrow kept happening.

I knew the streets.

That was almost inconvenient.

I did not need to ask directions.

I could go to Lyssa.

I could go to Hessa.

One of those choices involved a brass clasp.

The other involved a piece of failed magical garbage and a question I
had spent two days making worse.

I chose Lyssa.

Not because I had become wise.

Because I had been gone too long.

I made it three streets before realizing I was still carrying the
blue-lamp piece.

"Fuck."

I turned around.

At the hall, Pell was in the doorway.

He saw me.

He saw the wrapped glass in my hand.

He laughed so hard he had to hold the frame.

"Shut up."

"You went home with the lamp."

"I noticed."

"Did Lyssa want it?"

"I didn't get there."

"You could give it to her."

"No."

"Romantic."

"Fuck you."

Nessa appeared behind him.

She took the glass.

"Anything else?"

I checked.

Bag.

Clasp.

Throw blank.

Crutches.

Me.

"No."

"Go."

I went.

This time I made it farther.

The streets near Lyssa's usual place were busier than I remembered.

Or maybe I had forgotten.

A fruit seller had moved to the opposite corner. A sign over a tailor's
shop had acquired a tiny glamour that made the painted needle flash
silver when you passed beneath it.

I almost stopped.

I did not.

I reached the door.

Then I stood there.

That was stupid.

I had performed for rooms full of people.

I had argued about money with children.

I had been tied to a board.

I had bought educational garbage from a woman who thought I was an
idiot.

I could knock on a door.

I knocked.

Nobody answered.

Of course.

I waited.

Knocked again.

Nothing.

A woman coming down the street looked at me.

"You looking for Lyssa?"

"Yes."

"She's out."

"Where?"

The woman shifted the basket on her hip.

"North side, I think. Said something about cloth."

That could mean anything.

"When?"

"This morning."

"Right."

She looked at my bag.

"You Greg?"

I stared at her.

"Yes."

"She got your letter."

Then she walked past me.

I turned.

"Which one?"

She looked back.

"What?"

"Nothing."

She kept going.

I stood outside Lyssa's empty door.

She had gotten a letter.

At least one.

Maybe both.

I had come home.

She was somewhere else.

That felt correct.

I sat on the step because my arms hurt.

The brass clasp was still in my coat.

The failed throw blank was still in my pocket.

Hessa was somewhere in Carrow too.

Tomorrow, I could make her frown.

Tonight, apparently, I had to find Lyssa.

I smiled.

Then I got up.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 175

## THE GIFT-GIVER

The woman with the basket had said north side.

That was not an address.

I knew this because I went north and found six streets, two cloth shops,
a dyer's yard, three women carrying folded linen, and no Lyssa.

The first cloth shop had blue bolts stacked to the ceiling and a
prepared measuring cord that crawled flat across the counter when the
shopkeeper tapped one end. I watched it straighten itself.

"Buying?"

"No."

"Then don't lean on the wool."

I moved.

The second shop knew Lyssa.

"She was here."

"When?"

The woman behind the counter looked at the window.

"Before."

That was useful.

"Did she say where she was going?"

"Yes."

I waited.

The woman folded a length of brown cloth.

"Are you going to ask?"

"I thought I did."

"You asked if she said."

"Where did she go?"

"Marra's."

"Where's Marra?"

She pointed with the cloth.

"Two lanes. Green door. Don't knock on the red one."

"Why?"

"That's Sen's."

I did not know Sen.

Apparently that was reason enough.

Marra's green door stood open.

I heard Lyssa before I saw her.

"No, if you cut it there, it will pull when she lifts her arm."

Another woman said, "She doesn't lift her arm."

"Everybody lifts their arm."

"Not like that."

"Marra."

"Fine."

I stopped in the doorway.

Lyssa stood beside a table covered in gray cloth. She had one end pinned
between two fingers while a shorter woman leaned over it with chalk.
Another woman, older, sat by the window unpicking a seam from a dark
green dress.

None of them looked at me.

I had traveled for weeks.

I had performed in markets, mills, halls, yards, and beside livestock.

I had crossed bridges.

I had slept under wagons.

I had come home.

Lyssa was arguing about a sleeve.

Good.

The shorter woman looked up first.

"Door."

"I'm not blocking it."

"You are."

I moved.

Lyssa turned.

She stopped.

Not for long.

Her face changed in a way I could not separate fast enough.

Then she put the cloth down.

"You."

"Me."

"You're back."

"Apparently."

She crossed the room.

I had time to think I should say something.

Then she put both arms around me.

That solved it.

I held her.

My crutch slipped against the floor.

The shorter woman said, "Careful."

Lyssa caught me before I fell.

"Excellent," she said into my shoulder. "You've been home thirty
seconds."

"I was doing well."

"You smell."

"I've been traveling."

"I know."

She pulled back enough to look at me.

Her hands stayed on my arms.

"You look terrible."

"Thank you."

"Not terrible terrible."

"Better."

"Tired."

"I am."

"Thin."

"I ate."

"Did you?"

"Mostly."

The shorter woman cleared her throat.

Lyssa looked over.

"Marra, this is Greg."

Marra looked at me.

"The road one?"

I looked at Lyssa.

She said, "Apparently."

Marra nodded once.

"Don't bleed on the cloth."

"I'm not bleeding."

"Good."

The older woman by the window said, "Yet."

Lyssa laughed.

I had missed that.

That was inconvenient.

"What are you doing?" I asked.

"Helping Marra fix a dress she promised yesterday."

Marra said, "I did not promise yesterday."

"You said tomorrow."

"Yesterday."

"Exactly."

Marra pointed chalk at her.

"You came here voluntarily."

"I know."

The older woman held up the green dress.

"This sleeve is wrong too."

Lyssa closed her eyes.

I said, "I can go."

"No."

"I can wait."

"No."

"You appear busy."

"I am."

That was not the same as wanting me gone.

I understood that now.

Mostly.

Lyssa pointed at a stool near the wall.

"Sit."

I sat.

For the next twenty minutes, nobody asked about my journey.

Marra cut cloth.

Lyssa pinned a sleeve.

The older woman, whose name was Jessa, complained that whoever had sewn
the green dress originally hated shoulders.

I watched.

A little prepared warming plate sat under a pot near the back wall.
Every few minutes Marra put her chalk down, touched the plate, and held
her fingers over it.

That was all the magic in the room.

The rest was needles.

At one point Lyssa glanced at me.

"You're still here."

"I was told to sit."

"Good."

Marra said, "He learns."

"Slowly."

"I've improved."

Lyssa looked at my bag.

"What happened to that?"

"Nothing."

"That seam."

"Serra fixed it."

"Who is Serra?"

"Actor."

Lyssa's eyebrows moved.

"She fixed your bag."

"After I fixed it."

"Ah."

"Mine was structural."

Lyssa smiled.

"What did she call it?"

I stared at her.

"How do you know she called it something?"

"Because I've met you."

"Criminal."

Marra laughed.

"She called the stitches criminal."

Lyssa nodded.

"Correct."

"I had been on the road."

"Needles work on roads."

"Not well."

"Did you try sewing while the wagon was moving?"

"No."

I had.

Not the bag.

Something else.

I decided that did not count.

The dress eventually became acceptable.

Marra paid Lyssa with a folded piece of pale cloth and what looked like
two copper.

Lyssa put both away without showing me.

Good.

She had not been helping for fun.

Outside, the light had started going gold between the buildings.

Lyssa took my bag before I could object.

"I can carry that."

"I know."

"Give it back."

"No."

"I have crutches."

"Yes."

"That is why I have a bag."

"Greg."

"What?"

"You walked here from wherever you came from."

"East Market Hall."

"Before that."

"Halver."

"Before that."

"Rellin."

She looked at me.

"Dast."

"Keep going."

"Kest."

"Give me the bag."

I let her carry it.

We walked south.

Not toward her place at first.

She turned into a food lane.

"I ate."

"When?"

"Morning."

"That's not what I asked."

"Road house."

"What did you eat?"

"Beans."

"And?"

"Bread."

"And?"

"Beans."

She bought two meat buns.

I paid for mine.

She noticed.

"You have money."

"I work."

"Do you?"

"Professionally."

"At what?"

"Waiting, mostly."

She handed me the bun.

I bit it too soon and burned my mouth.

Lyssa watched.

"Professional."

"Fuck you."

"Missed you too."

I nearly choked.

She smiled and kept walking.

That reminded me.

"The letter."

"Which one?"

I stopped.

She took another bite.

"Which one?"

"I got two."

"Both?"

"Unless you sent more."

"No."

"The first one made you sound sensible."

"I was sensible."

"The second one said you didn't share apples with Marek."

"He didn't deserve them."

"I don't know who Marek is."

"Exactly."

She walked.

I caught up.

"You got the Dast one?"

"Yesterday."

"That was fast."

"It was a letter, Greg. Not a wagon."

"It was on a wagon."

"Probably."

"Did you write back?"

"Yes."

I stared at her.

"Where?"

"East Market Hall."

"When?"

"This morning."

I turned my head toward the direction of the hall.

Lyssa caught my sleeve.

"Finish eating before you go anywhere."

"I wasn't going anywhere."

"Good."

I ate.

Her reply was probably sitting at the hall I had left less than an hour
ago.

That was irritating.

Also funny.

I had traveled faster than the answer.

We reached her place.

Inside, nothing had arranged itself around my absence.

A cup sat on the table.

A folded shawl lay over the chair.

There were three onions in a bowl and one had gone soft.

A book was open facedown where it should not have been.

I knew better than to say that.

Lyssa put my bag down.

"Bath."

"Now?"

"Yes."

"I just got here."

"You arrived dirty."

"I can sit dirty."

"You can sit after."

I obeyed.

The water was not hot enough to be luxurious.

It was hot enough.

I washed road dust out of places I had stopped noticing road dust could
be.

When I came back, Lyssa had put bread, cheese, and sliced onion on the
table.

"You bought food."

"I own food."

"Right."

"You've forgotten houses."

"Some."

I sat.

My body noticed the chair was not moving.

That was almost unpleasant.

Lyssa sat across from me.

For a while we ate.

Then she said, "How long were you supposed to be gone?"

"I don't remember."

"You told me a few days."

"That sounds wrong now."

"It sounded wrong then."

"I didn't know."

"I know."

No accusation.

That made it worse for a second.

Then she reached across and stole my cheese.

That fixed it.

"There was a goat," I said.

She chewed.

"Of course."

"It ate mounting cloth."

"What is mounting cloth?"

"Cloth for mounting."

"Helpful."

"For the Sword."

"You were the sword."

"Sometimes."

"You wrote that."

"I did?"

"Not clearly."

"That sounds like me."

"You also performed beside cheese."

"Yes."

"And livestock."

"Yes."

"And cider."

"Yes."

"Was any of this intentional?"

"Mostly."

She laughed.

I told her about the north arcade wind.

Not the whole thing.

Just the cheese woman and the carts.

Then the goose came out.

"A real goose is bad theatre," I said.

Lyssa stopped.

"What?"

"We didn't use one."

"You stole a goose."

"We did not steal a goose."

"You tried."

"No."

"Pell tried?"

"He suggested."

"Who is Pell?"

"Props."

"Person or job?"

"Both."

She looked delighted.

I told her about the fox.

That took less time.

"It sounded like someone being murdered."

"Foxes do."

"I know that now."

"You've never heard one?"

"Apparently not correctly."

She frowned slightly.

"What does that mean?"

"I don't know."

That was true.

I ate bread.

Then I remembered the clasp.

Not because of anything romantic.

Because it dug into my chest when I leaned forward.

"Oh."

Lyssa looked at me.

"What?"

"I bought you something."

Her expression changed immediately.

Not softer.

More suspicious.

"Why?"

"I saw it."

"That's not an answer."

"It is the whole answer."

I reached inside my coat and took out the wrapped little packet.

The wrapping looked worse than when I bought it.

Of course it did.

I put it on the table.

Lyssa looked at it.

"Is it alive?"

"No."

"Magic?"

"No."

"Food?"

"No."

"Then why are you nervous?"

"I'm not."

"You've performed tied to a board."

"Mounted."

"Your letter said tied."

"That was editorial simplification."

She opened the wrapping.

The brass clasp lay in her palm.

Two small leaves.

Nothing expensive.

Nothing magical.

Just brass worked carefully enough that the veins showed when the light
caught them.

Lyssa touched one leaf with her thumb.

I suddenly wanted to explain the price.

That would have been terrible.

So I said nothing.

"You carried this the whole way?"

"I bought it after the first northern show."

"That was before Dast."

"Yes."

"Before the mill?"

"I think so."

"You think?"

"There were many places."

She looked at me.

Then at the clasp.

Then she stood.

For one horrifying second I thought she hated it.

She went to the small mirror.

Her hair was loose enough that the clasp was not useful there.

She fastened it instead at the edge of her shawl.

It worked.

She looked at it.

"Good?"

I said, "Yes."

"That's all?"

"What do you want?"

"I don't know. You looked like you were going to give a speech."

"I was trying not to."

"Good."

She came back and kissed me.

That was better than a speech.

Later, I found out I had fallen asleep sitting up.

I knew this because I woke with my neck bent against the wall and
Lyssa's foot under my thigh.

It was dark.

A prepared street lamp outside made a pale bar across the floor.

Lyssa was reading.

"You slept."

"I noticed."

"You snored."

"I don't."

"You did."

"Road damage."

"Permanent."

I shifted.

Everything hurt.

"Bed?"

She closed the book.

"Eventually."

"Why eventually?"

"Because you're awake now."

That was fair.

I looked at the brass leaves at her shoulder.

She had not taken the clasp off.

I liked that more than I intended to.

"What's tomorrow?" she asked.

"The hall."

"What time?"

"I don't know."

"Useful."

"Teren was talking about tomorrow before we finished unloading."

"Of course he was."

"And Hessa."

Lyssa looked at me.

"Tomorrow?"

"Yes."

"Did you practice?"

"No."

"At all?"

"No."

She studied me.

"Good."

"That sounded surprised."

"It was."

"I follow rules."

"You follow rules after arguing with them."

"Still counts."

"What are you taking her?"

I reached for my trousers where I had left them folded badly.

Lyssa said, "No."

"I need the pocket."

"You need sleep."

"There's a thing."

"Tomorrow."

"It's garbage."

"Excellent. Tomorrow."

I lay back down.

"You'll like it."

"I already don't."

"It cost one copper."

"Greg."

"What?"

"Sleep."

I did.

Morning in Carrow was louder than road morning.

Road morning had birds, horses, wagons, people pissing behind things.

Carrow had bells.

Cart wheels.

Vendors.

Somebody below shouting about hot cakes.

A prepared sign across the lane brightened from gray to yellow when the
sun reached it.

Lyssa was already dressed.

The brass clasp was gone from the shawl.

I noticed.

Then I saw it fastened at the side of her hair.

I tried not to look too pleased.

She caught me.

"Don't."

"I didn't say anything."

"Your face did."

"Good clasp."

"Go to work."

I ate one hot cake she bought downstairs.

Then another.

She had somewhere to be.

I did not ask if I could come.

That felt important enough not to think about.

At the corner, she kissed me once.

"When are you done?"

"I don't know."

"Find out."

"Yes."

"Are you leaving again?"

"No."

That came out too fast.

Lyssa looked at me.

I corrected.

"Not today."

"Better."

"Probably not tomorrow."

"Greg."

"I don't know."

"I know."

She touched the clasp once, then pointed at me.

"Find out."

"Yes."

She went east.

I went toward East Market Hall.

The reply letter was there.

Rinna had put it under a cup so Pell would not touch it.

I did not read it immediately.

That was growth.

I put it in my bag.

Teren was in the hall with two actors I did not know and a man arguing
about chairs.

Nessa had half the costume chest open.
