Pell was on the floor with the wooden fish.

Davin was not there.

Marek was eating.

Of course.

Teren saw me.

"Tonight."

"What?"

"Show."

"What am I?"

"Shopkeeper."

"Only?"

"For now."

"Good."

He looked at me.

"What?"

"You sound disappointed."

"I'm not."

"You are."

"I have another thing."

"What thing?"

"Guild."

He waved me away.

"Be back by four."

That was the entire negotiation.

I went.

Hessa was not waiting for me either.

She had someone else at her table.

A woman with a wrapped forearm sat in my usual chair while Hessa
examined a row of tiny dark marks on the skin.

I stopped in the doorway.

Hessa looked up once.

"You're back."

"Yes."

"Sit outside."

"Hello to you too."

"Outside."

I sat outside.

For twenty-five minutes.

The woman came out with her arm rewrapped and instructions I did not
hear.

Hessa called, "Greg."

I went in.

The room had not changed enough.

That was becoming a theme.

The suspended-thread apparatus was still shelved.

My old notes were not on the table.

Hessa looked at me.

"You look tired."

"Lyssa said terrible."

"She was being kind."

"Good."

"Did you draw?"

"No."

"Shape?"

"No."

"Test?"

"No."

"Anything I prohibited?"

"No."

She watched me for another second.

"Good."

I sat.

Then I took the failed throw blank from my pocket and put it on her
table.

Hessa looked down.

She did not touch it.

Her mouth tightened.

That was the frown.

"What is that?"

"Educational garbage."

Her eyes lifted to mine.

"That is not a category."

"It was one copper."

The frown got worse.

I smiled.

"I have a question."

"I assumed."

"It's about how little something has to be real."

Hessa looked at the metal again.

Then at me.

"Specific question."

"I'm getting there."

"Ask it."

I leaned forward.

The failed clasp sat between us.

Completely inert.

Completely useless.

For the first time since I had left Carrow, I was exactly where I was
allowed to make the question worse.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 176

## THE QUESTIONER

"So," I said.

Hessa waited.

There were people who made waiting feel patient.

Hessa made it feel like I had already wasted something.

"The blue lamp makes the light blue."

"Yes."

"You haven't seen it."

"You told me what it does."

"Right. But it doesn't make the room cold."

"I would hope not."

"The room feels cold."

"To whom?"

"The audience."

"Did you ask them?"

"No."

"Then the room felt cold to you."

"It did."

"Good. Continue."

I disliked this already.

"There was rain."

"Inside?"

"Outside."

"Greg."

"The wall was pale. Serra was in the light. The light was blue. It
looked cold."

"So several real things produced an impression."

"Yes."

"That is theatre."

"Some of it."

"What part isn't?"

I pointed at the failed throw blank.

"The magic."

Hessa looked at it.

"The blue lamp uses a prepared piece."

"Yes."

"And this is not the blue lamp."

"No. That's sound."

"This is sound?"

"It was supposed to be."

"Supposed to be is doing a great deal of work."

"It doesn't do anything."

"Good."

"Why is that good?"

"Because I can touch it."

She picked it up.

Varo's failed blank looked smaller in Hessa's hand. She turned it toward
the window, then reached for a little magnifying lens from the shelf
behind her. The lens had a brass rim and no magic that I could see. She
held the blank beneath it.

"Who made this?"

"Varo. Rellin. Blue shutters."

"Profession?"

"Instrument maker. Repairs. Prepared fittings."

"Did she tell you what failed?"

"Channel marked. Bias never set."

Hessa turned the blank.

"That is consistent."

"You can tell?"

"I can tell there is a marked preparation line and no completed bias
structure."

"What's a bias structure?"

"The thing you are not learning today."

"I was asking."

"And I answered."

She put the lens down.

"Anything held in it?"

"No."

"Did she say that?"

"She said it was garbage."

"Good maker."

"Educational garbage."

"Less good."

"One copper."

"I remember."

She put the blank on the table.

"Why did you buy it?"

"So I could look at it."

Hessa's face changed slightly.

Not approval.

Less disapproval.

That was probably the highest available grade.

"And what did looking tell you?"

"That I don't know what I'm looking at."

"Excellent."

"Fuck you."

"Also that."

I leaned back.

The room smelled like old paper, clean metal, and the sharp soap Hessa
used on the table. Outside the door, somebody walked past carrying a
rack of six narrow glass tubes. One glowed faintly amber at the bottom.
Nobody screamed.

I said, "The throw clasp doesn't make another sound."

"According to the maker."

"It changes enough about the sound that you put it somewhere else."

"You think."

"Varo thinks."

"Better."

"And the room helps."

"What room?"

"Her shop."

Hessa looked at me.

"You're changing examples."

"They're connected."

"That is what worries me."

I ignored that.

"The cheap one on her door wasn't very good. Pell heard it wrong."

"Pell?"

"Props."

"Person?"

"Both."

"Of course."

"But the door, the walls, where we were standing, all of that made it
work better. The clasp didn't have to do everything."

Hessa folded her hands.

"And?"

"And the blue lamp doesn't have to make cold. A real goose doesn't have
to be onstage to make a goose."

She blinked.

I kept going because stopping would have made it worse.

"A fox sounds wrong until someone tells you fox."

"What did you think it was?"

"Someone dying."

"Reasonable."

"Then Pell said fox and it sounded like a fox."

"The sound changed?"

"No."

"So."

"So what?"

"You tell me."

"The thing didn't change."

"Correct."

"I did."

"Possibly."

"That's annoying."

"Good."

I looked at the blank again.

"What if the magic only has to do one small real thing?"

Hessa did not answer immediately.

That was different.

I leaned forward.

"Not the whole thing. Not make the room cold. Not make another sound.
Not make a goose."

"Please stop making geese."

"I never made a goose."

"Continue."

"What if I don't need to make something big happen? What if I only need
to make one tiny thing happen, and then everything else is..."

I moved my hand.

Hessa waited.

"Theatre," I finished.

"No."

I stared at her.

"That was the good version."

"It was not."

"Why?"

"Because you have changed questions again."

She pointed at the blank.

"That object is prepared structure. Most of whatever useful behavior a
completed version has was designed into it by someone who knows how to
make one."

She pointed toward the window.

"Your blue lamp changes light."

"Yes."

"The audience's interpretation of that light is not a magical effect."

"Yes."

"Your own external work is a third problem."

"Yes."

"Say it without lying."

I frowned.

"I wasn't lying."

"You were making them sound like one thing."

"That's theatre."

"No. That is irritating."

I laughed.

Hessa did not.

I tried again.

"I want to know if I can make a smaller external change than we were
trying before."

There.

Hessa looked at me for several seconds.

"That is a question."

"I had a question before."

"You had weather, a fox, a goose, an instrument fitting, a lamp, and an
opinion."

"The opinion was good."

"The question is better."

She stood.

I looked toward the shelf with the suspended-thread apparatus.

Hessa said, "Not the threads."

"I can look."

"You can look while we use something better."

She moved past the shelf and opened a low cabinet.

"What time do you need to leave?"

"Four."

"What happens at four?"

"Teren becomes angry."

"Useful measurement."

"Show tonight."

"Doing what?"

"Shopkeeper."

"Of course."

She took out a shallow wooden box.

Inside were little squares of thin paper, two flat pieces of clear
glass, chalk, a narrow wooden frame, and several small metal washers.

None of it looked magical.

I liked that.

"What is that?"

"Things."

"That is not a category."

"It is in my room."

"Unfair."

"Sit."

She set the wooden frame on the table.

It was about the length of my hand and twice as wide. She laid one piece
of glass across the top, then slid two small folded paper tabs
underneath it on separate chalk marks. The glass did not touch the tabs.
It rested on the frame above them, making a low clear roof.

"Breath shield," I said.

"Yes."

"I knew that."

"You are breathing."

"Professionally."

"Stop."

She put one washer on each corner of the frame.

"Table movement?"

"Partly. Also because you touch things."

"I don't."

She looked at me.

"I touch some things."

"Both tabs are cut from the same sheet. Same size. Same fold. One
target, one control."

She marked a small circle beside the left tab.

"Why not glass all around?"

"Because I have an hour, not a workshop."

"I have more than an hour."

"You have until four."

"I could be late."

"No."

That surprised me.

Hessa looked at me.

"You have work."

"Yes."

"Then go to work at four."

"Three forty-five."

"Three thirty."

"Why?"

"Because you walk."

"Rude."

"Accurate."

She pulled my old chair into place.

"We are not proving your theory."

"I don't have a theory."

"Excellent. Keep it that way."

"What are we proving?"

"Nothing."

"That's inspiring."

"We are asking whether you can produce a small external displacement
under a cleaner condition than your previous attempts."

"That's what I said."

"No."

"It is."

"You said goose."

"Related."

"No."

I smiled.

She did not.

Then the smile went away because she said, "Draw."

The word changed the room.

Not dramatically.

Nothing glowed.

No prepared object sang.

I had simply not heard Hessa tell me to do that in weeks.

I put my hands flat on my thighs.

Breathed.

Not too much.

I knew what reaching felt like now.

I also knew what not reaching felt like.

The first few times with Hessa, I had expected mana to arrive like
something entering a room.

It did not.

It was closer to finding a pressure I had been standing inside the whole
time and learning which part of myself was allowed to answer it.

I drew minimally.

Hessa watched.

"Enough."

I stopped.

The draw was clean.

Not impressive.

Not difficult either.

That bothered me more than difficulty would have.

Weeks on the road, no practice, and my body still knew the shape of the
instruction.

Hessa wrote something.

"Twenty-one?" I asked.

"Yes."

I had not meant to sound pleased.

I did anyway.

"Again?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because we are testing something else."

She pointed at the target tab.

"Shape toward that."

"Move it?"

"Not yet."

"What am I shaping?"

"The smallest directed form you can hold without spilling it."

"That sounds like moving it."

"It is not."

I breathed again.

The mana was already gone from the draw. I drew minimally a second time
only after she told me to, then held it under her instruction and tried
to narrow what I was doing.

Hessa stopped me twice before I had anything.

"Too broad."

Again.

"You're pushing."

"I'm not."

"You are."

"How can I push if nothing is moving?"

"With enthusiasm."

"That's not a magical term."

"It is today."

Third time, I found something narrower.

Not a line.

Not a thread.

I was not going back to thread.

A direction, maybe.

That was too pretty.

A preference.

That was worse.

I held it.

Hessa watched my wrist.

Then my face.

Then the tab.

"Stop."

I released.

"That was good."

I looked at her.

"Actually?"

"Cleaner."

"Seventeen?"

"Yes."

That pleased me more.

Then Hessa moved the entire apparatus away.

"What?"

"Rest."

"I'm fine."

"I know."

"Then why?"

"Because you have started wanting the paper to move."

"That is the test."

"Later."

I hated her.

For six minutes.

During the six minutes, I remembered Lyssa's letter.

I took it from my bag.

Hessa was writing.

"Can I read?"

"Can you do it quietly?"

"No."

"Then no."

I opened it anyway.

Lyssa's letter was shorter than mine.

That seemed rude.

She said she was glad I had reached Dast without being eaten by
anything, which I had never suggested was a possibility. She said Marra
had finally admitted the gray cloth was wrong and they were replacing
it. She said the woman downstairs had started asking whether "the road
actor" was coming back, which explained yesterday.

Then:

You said you miss me. Good. Come back before I get used to having the
whole bed.

Below that:

Also stop being cruel to Marek about apples. I don't know him but I have
decided he deserved one.

I folded the letter.

Hessa said, "Bad news?"

"Terrible."

"Good."

"Lyssa has taken Marek's side."

"I don't know who Marek is."

"Nobody does."

Hessa moved the frame back.

"Ready?"

I put the letter away.

"Yes."

This time she marked the target tab's starting position with a fine
chalk line.

Then she marked the control.

"Your task is not to convince me it moved."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"Probably."

"No."

"Fine."

"Your task is to attempt one small directional influence on the marked
target. Nothing else."

"How far?"

"I don't care."

"That's suspicious."

"If it moves at all, we measure. If it does not, we record that."

"What if it almost moves?"

"It does not."

"That's harsh."

"Reality often is."

I settled.

Draw.

Minimal.

Shape.

Small.

The urge to perform the attempt was immediate.

That was new.

Not perform for Hessa.

Perform for the result.

I wanted the tab to twitch at the right moment. I wanted the still
control beside it. I wanted the clean little story.

Target moves.

Control does not.

Greg did magic.

Perfect.

I could see the scene before anything happened.

That made me distrust it.

I stopped.

Hessa said, "Why?"

"I was making it good."

She stared at me.

Then she leaned back.

"Explain."

"I wanted it to move right."

"There is no right."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

She tapped the table once.

"Again."

I drew.

Shaped.

Held the smallest directed form I could manage.

Then tried to let it touch the world.

Nothing happened.

I did not push harder.

That felt like failure.

It also felt correct.

"Stop," Hessa said.

I stopped.

We both looked at the tabs.

Neither had moved.

"External attempt four," she said.

"Nothing."

"Correct."

I exhaled.

The target tab trembled.

I pointed.

"It moved."

"You breathed."

"I know."

"Good."

"I was joking."

"No, you weren't."

"Mostly."

Hessa wrote.

I looked at the paper.

I had expected disappointment to feel worse.

Instead I was annoyed by the tab.

That seemed healthier.

"Again?" I asked.

"No."

"One attempt?"

"One controlled external attempt today."

"We have time."

"We also have a useful failure."

"Those are cheap."

"They are if you waste them."

She took the glass roof off and picked up the target tab.

"You did two things better than before."

"Only two?"

"You kept the shaping smaller."

"Good."

"And you stopped when you noticed yourself constructing the result."

I looked at her.

"That's not magic."

"No."

"Then it doesn't count."

"It counts for me."

That was irritatingly close to praise.

I touched the failed throw blank.

"What about this?"

Hessa slid it toward me.

"Take your garbage."

"You don't want it?"

"I have better garbage."

"Can I bring it next time?"

"If you have a question about prepared structure."

"I do."

"Then write the question before you arrive."

"Why?"

"So I do not have to hear about geese."

"The goose is important."

"Ask your players."

That shut me up.

Mostly.

I put the blank back in its pocket.

"Next time?"

"Two days."

"I have theatre."

"At this exact hour?"

"I don't know."

"Find out."

Everyone was telling me that now.

"What are we doing?"

"Repeating this."

"The paper?"

"Something similar."

"Can we make it smaller?"

Hessa looked at me.

"The effect?"

"Yes."

"It was zero."

"Right."

"Hard to make smaller."

"You know what I mean."

"I do."

She closed the wooden box.

"We can make the question narrower."

That was probably what I meant.

It sounded worse when she said it.

I stood.

"Twenty-one draws. Seventeen shaping."

"Successful supervised minimal draws," Hessa said. "Successful
supervised deliberate shaping attempts."

"Yes."

"Four supervised external-effect attempts."

"With no established external effect."

"Correct."

"I remember."

"Say it anyway."

"No established external magical effect."

"Good."

"No spell."

"Correct."

"No Barrier."

"Correct."

"Independent work still prohibited."

"Very."

"I bought inert garbage instead."

"I am trying to reward that choice."

"You have an unusual face for reward."

"Go to work."

It was three twenty-seven.

I went.

East Market Hall smelled different when I came in through the side door.

Not actually.

Paint.

Old cloth.

Lamp oil.

Dust.

People.

But after Hessa's room, everything felt dishonest.

That was unfair to theatre.

Theatre was honest about being dishonest.

I was still deciding whether that sentence meant anything when Nessa
shoved a folded coat into my chest.

"Put that down."

"What?"

"Your bag."

I had carried it into the costume lane.

I moved it.

"Where?"

"Not there."

I moved it again.

"Greg."

"You're becoming Hessa."

"I don't know who that is."

"Good."

She took the coat back.

The hall was fuller than the touring company had been. Two men were
rigging a painted interior wall I remembered from before we left. A
woman I had seen once in the prop room was sorting cups by size. Another
actor was walking a line under his breath while Pell tried to get him to
lift one foot so he could retrieve a strap.

Marek was not eating.

That concerned me.

Teren found me.

"Shopkeeper. Second."

"Second what?"

"Piece."

"What first?"

"King."

"Who's King?"

"Not you."

"Good."

"You're also carrying the ledger on."

"That's not Shopkeeper."

"It is now."

"Why?"

"Because the person who was carrying it isn't here."

"Who?"

Teren had already turned away.

Home.

I changed.

The Shopkeeper coat fit differently after the road.

Or I did.

I found the ledger.

Then I noticed a small round hole low in the wall behind the side cloth.

I had seen it before.

I crouched.

A leather tube disappeared through it.

Pell appeared beside me.

"Don't."

"I'm looking."

"That's the ghost."

"The whole ghost?"

"The mouth."

I looked at him.

"Where's the other end?"

He pointed vaguely beneath the stage.

"Depends."

"On what?"

"Where Nessa puts it."

"Does Teren know you explain things like this?"

"No."

"Good."

Pell left.

I looked at the hole again.

Nothing magical.

A hole.

A tube.

A voice from somewhere it should not be.

Enough, if you did not know where to look.

"Greg!"

Teren.

I stood too fast and nearly hit my head.

"Here."

"Why are you on the floor?"

"Ghost."

He looked at the hole.

"Later."

That was becoming another category of education.

The show started.

King first.

I waited in the side corridor with the ledger under my arm.

The audience was quieter than Dast.

Quieter than the mill.

Quieter than the private house in a different way.

They knew where the stage was.

They had come to watch it.

Nobody was carrying turnips through the performance.

That should have made everything easier.

I entered too large.

Not physically.

The first line came out pitched for a market edge.

The room gave it back to me.

Too much.

Marek, playing a minor official, looked at me.

Not Greg.

Shopkeeper.

But I knew the look.

Smaller.

I adjusted.

Three lines later I rushed a pause because I expected someone to walk
away.

Nobody did.

The silence stayed.

I had forgotten audiences could wait.

That was embarrassing.

Then the scene settled.

The ledger was real wood and paper.

The debt was not real.

The irritation was real enough.

A woman in the second row leaned toward the man beside her before I had
finished a sentence. He whispered something. She covered a laugh.

I did not know what they thought was happening between us.

I did not need to.

Marek said, "I have already explained the circumstances."

"You explained circumstances," I said. "You have not explained money."

That landed.

Not huge.

Clean.

I let it.

Later, I nearly used the road version of a line that depended on a
constable who was not in this cut.

I felt it arrive.

Wrong room.

Wrong version.

I let it die.

Marek continued.

Good.

At the end, applause.

Not a lot.

Enough.

I came offstage and Teren said, "First entrance was shit."

"I know."

"Second half good."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

He left.

I sat on a prop chest.

Pell was under the stage.

Somebody above me dragged a chair.

The ghost tube shifted beside my boot.

I thought about the paper tab.

Hessa had covered it with glass so my breath could not lie for me.

Here, we put a tube through a wall so a voice could.

That was not the same thing.

I knew that.

It still felt close enough to be annoying.

Rinna passed with a small cash box.

"You're in tomorrow."

"What?"

"Maybe."

"That's not in."

"Then you're learning."

She kept walking.

I took Lyssa's letter from my bag and read the line about the bed again.

Then I folded it and put it away before Pell could crawl out and ask
what I was smiling at.

He crawled out anyway.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"That's suspicious."

"Go be props."

"I am props."

"Exactly."

Someone called him.

He went.

I sat there another minute.

Magic had done nothing today.

The show had convinced a room of several things that were not true.

Neither fact made the other simpler.

At four tomorrow, I might be Shopkeeper again.

In two days, Hessa wanted another piece of paper not to move.

For once, both sounded like work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 177

## THE STAGEHAND

The ghost had a kink in it.

I found that out because Pell said, "Talk."

I put my mouth near the wooden cup.

"What?"

From somewhere behind the painted wall, Pell shouted, "Not you."

"I am talking."

"Other end."

"You told me to hold this end."

"I told you to hold the ghost."

"Which end is the ghost?"

Nessa's voice came from under the stage.

"The end he didn't give you."

Pell looked offended.

"I was getting there."

"You were not."

It was morning.

East Market Hall had already become impossible.

A painted wall leaned against two braces in the middle of the floor.
Someone had hung three shirts from the balcony rail. A woman I did not
know was arguing with one of the lamp men about whether a prepared
warming stone belonged in costumes or properties. He said properties
because it was a stone. She said costumes because it went inside a coat.

Neither asked me.

Teren crossed behind them carrying a stool.

"Ghost in the third," he said.

Then he kept walking.

Pell looked at me.

"You heard him."

"I heard words."

"Tube."

"Why me?"

"You have arms."

"I have one leg."

"The tube doesn't."

That was unfortunately reasonable.

The ghost was twenty feet of narrow leather tube with a wooden
mouthpiece at one end and a flatter wooden opening at the other. The
leather was old enough to have opinions. It wanted to bend where it had
always bent and nowhere else.

Pell had given me the mouthpiece.

Nessa wanted the flat end.

I passed it down.

"Where?"

"Here."

Her hand appeared between the stage boards.

I gave her the end.

"No."

"You said here."

"I meant me."

"That is here."

"Greg."

I lowered it farther.

She took it.

Pell crouched beside me and fed the tube through the low hole I had
noticed yesterday.

"Don't twist it."

"I'm not."

"You are."

"That's the tube."

"Tube doesn't twist itself."

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

We both looked at the tube.

It had twisted itself.

"Fine," Pell said.

We fed more through.

The third piece was something called The Mourning House.

I had never seen it.

Apparently everyone else had.

That was becoming normal.

A woman named Veya played a widow who had inherited a house from an
uncle she hated. Marek played the uncle in the first scene and then
died. This pleased him because it meant he could spend most of the piece
backstage.

The dead uncle spoke twice after death.

That was the ghost.

"Why not just put Pell behind the wall?" I asked.

"Because the wall moves," Nessa said from below.

"Why not put him under the stage?"

"Because the audience can hear under the stage."

"Why can't they hear the tube?"

"They can."

I waited.

Nessa's head appeared through a gap beside the steps.

"They hear the wrong part."

That did not help.

Pell said, "It's obvious."

"Then explain it."

"No."

"Because you can't."

"Because Nessa will yell."

"I can hear you," Nessa said.

Pell whispered, "See?"

We routed the tube behind the painted wall, down through the low hole,
under the stage, and back up beside a dark hanging on the opposite side.

I thought the outlet should go farther.

"If it comes from over there," I said, pointing toward the rear corner,
"then it will sound more impossible."

Nessa looked at the corner.

"No."

"Why?"

"Mud."

"What?"

"Sound."

"That's not mud."

"It will be."

She took the flat outlet from me and fixed it behind the hanging less
than eight feet from where Veya would stand.

"That's too close."

"Good."

"How is close better?"

"Listen."

Pell went behind the wall.

Veya came onto the stage holding a cup.

She was maybe forty. I had seen her yesterday sorting nothing and
assumed she was crew.

She looked at the room.

"Where's my chair?"

Nobody answered.

"Where is my chair?"

A man on the balcony said, "King."

Veya looked up.

"Why?"

"King needed another."

"My dead uncle needs it."

Marek called from backstage, "I can die standing."

"You die in the first scene."

"I can do it."

"You're already dead in the third."

"Then I definitely don't need the chair."

Veya closed her eyes.

This problem had existed before I arrived.

Good.

Someone found another chair.

Pell said through the tube, "Veya."

His voice came from the hanging.

It sounded exactly like Pell speaking through a tube.

I laughed.

Pell emerged from behind the wall.

"What?"

"That was terrible."

"It was a test."

"You sounded like yourself in a bucket."

"It's leather."

"Leather bucket."

Nessa adjusted the outlet.

"Again."

Pell disappeared.

Veya stood beside the chair.

"Veya."

Still Pell.

Less bucket.

Veya turned toward the hanging before he finished saying her name.

Nessa said, "No."

Veya looked at her.

"What?"

"You're early."

"I heard him."

"So did everyone."

"That's why I looked."

"After."

Veya sighed.

Again.

Pell said, "Veya."

Veya waited.

Then turned.

It was better.

Not good.

Better.

Nessa lowered the nearest lamp.

The hall changed.

Only a little.

The hanging became less brown and more black.

She moved Veya's chair half a pace toward center.

Then she told Pell, "Less."

"Less what?"

"You."

"That's all I have."

"Find less."

Pell muttered something.

"Again."

This time the voice was quieter.

"Veya."

Veya did not turn immediately.

She stopped moving.

That was different.

She had been folding a cloth. Her hands stopped with the cloth half
open.

Then her eyes went toward the dark hanging.

Not her head.

Her eyes.

"Uncle?"

Pell did not answer.

Nothing happened.

I looked at the hanging.

There was nothing there.

I knew there was nothing there.

I had put the fucking tube there.

Still, for about half a second, the space beside it had somebody in it.

Then Pell coughed under the stage.

The person disappeared.

Veya said, "Excellent."

Nessa kicked the boards.

Pell said, "Sorry."

I was still looking at the empty space.

Nessa noticed.

She did not smile.

"Tube."

"What?"

"You're standing on it."

I moved my crutch.

I had been.

That afternoon I learned three more things about ghosts.

The first was that leather hated corners.

I routed the tube too tightly behind a brace because it hid better
there. Pell tried the line and sounded like a dying kettle.

Nessa made me pull the whole section loose.

"Visible," I said.

"To who?"

I stepped into the audience.

From the seats, the tube disappeared behind the painted edge.

From backstage, it looked obvious.

I had hidden it from the wrong people.

The second thing was that the outlet could not touch cloth.

It buzzed.

Not magically.

Just badly.

The third was that actors were part of the mechanism.

Veya got tired of waiting for Pell's second line and started
anticipating it.

Every time she did, the ghost got worse.

"You know it's coming," Nessa told her.

"Because we've done it six times."

"They don't."

She pointed at the empty seats.

Veya looked at them.

Then at Nessa.

"Fine."

The seventh time, she let herself not know.

That was better too.

Nobody explained why.

They had work.

By three, the hall had acquired an audience of people who did not pay.

A carpenter sat in the back while waiting for somebody to move the
painted wall.

Two costume women watched from the side.

A boy delivering lamp oil stayed through most of Mourning House until
someone realized he had not delivered the lamp oil.

The prepared warming stone was eventually declared costume property.

I never learned who won.

At some point Rinna found me under the stage with Pell.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Two copper."

"For what?"

She held them out.

"Yesterday."

I took them.

"Show?"

"Show."

"Company share?"

"Your local rate."

I put them away.

"What about tonight?"

"If you do it."

"Helpful."

She looked at Pell.

"You owe me a copper."

Pell said, "No."

"You broke the latch."

"It was already weak."

"You made it two pieces."

"That's how we found out."

Rinna held out her hand.

Pell stared at it.

I crawled away before the economics became violent.

Outside, Carrow had decided to be warm.

A fruit seller had a shallow cooling plate under cut melon. The plate's
worked edge glimmered once when she set a fresh tray on it, then
stopped. Beside her, a man sold warm beer because apparently not
everyone made good decisions.

I bought bread.

Marek found me.

"Food?"

"You have eyes."

"Share."

"No."

"Lyssa says I deserved the apple."

He stopped.

"Who is Lyssa?"

"Nobody."

"You said Lyssa."

"I did not."

"You did."

I walked away.

He followed.

"Who told Lyssa about the apple?"

"Lyssa."

"That doesn't answer anything."

"Good."

He bought his own bread.

Back inside, Teren had written the evening bill on a board.

SHORT KING

MOURNING HOUSE

SHOPKEEPER

A fourth line had been written and crossed out so hard I could not read
it.

I pointed.

"What was that?"

"No."

"What?"

"Exactly."

"Am I Shopkeeper?"

"Yes."

"Anything else?"

"Ghost."

"I'm not the ghost."

"You're carrying it."

"That's not acting."

Teren looked at me.

"I didn't say it was."

Good.

I carried the tube.

We reset it for the evening.

This time Nessa made me place the outlet.

I put it where she had put it.

She looked.

"Too low."

"It was there."

"No."

"It was."

"The hanging moved."

I looked.

Someone had retied it two fingers higher.

"That's ridiculous."

"Fix it."

I moved the outlet.

"Too far."

I moved it back.

"Stop moving it like you're angry."

"I am angry."

"At leather?"

"Currently."

She crouched, touched the outlet, and rotated it slightly toward the
plaster side wall.

"Why?"

"Because that wall gives some back."

"The room."

"What?"

"Nothing."

Nessa looked at me.

"Varo?"

"Yes."

"She charges too much."

"One silver six."

"For a basic throw?"

"Yes."

"Too much."

"Pell said it was fair."

"Pell buys broken hinges."

"I heard that," Pell said.

He was under the stage.

"Good."

The doors opened.

The audience came in.

Not huge.

East Market Hall was not new to them.

They talked.

Found seats.

Moved seats.

One man objected to a post and then sat behind it anyway.

A child touched the painted wall until her mother stopped her.

The first piece began.

I was crew.

That felt different from waiting.

During King, I moved the ghost tube farther from a costume basket
because someone had put the basket on it.

Then I held a door flat while a hinge pin went back in.

Then I was supposed to be ready at the tube for Mourning House.

I was not the voice.

Pell was.

I only had to make sure nothing crushed it.

That was easy.

Until the lamp-oil boy came back.

He put two cans exactly where the tube crossed behind the wall.

I moved them.

He moved them back.

"No."

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Not there."

"Why?"

"Ghost."

He looked at the floor.

"Where?"

"Exactly."

He picked up the cans.

I liked him.

Mourning House began.

Marek died well.

Too well.

He added a hand twitch after the fall.

Veya stepped on it.

The audience laughed.

He stayed dead.

Professional.

Then the house became quiet.

Not actually quiet.

Someone coughed.

A bench creaked.

A child whispered.

But the piece wanted quiet, so the room began cooperating.

Veya sat.

Folded the cloth.

Stopped.

Pell spoke.

"Veya."

The voice came from the dark side.

I knew where he was.

I knew the tube path.

I knew the outlet.

I had adjusted it.

A woman in the third row turned toward the hanging.

Then the man beside her did.

Veya's hands stopped.

Her eyes moved.

The empty place filled.

Not with a ghost.

With everyone's attention.

That was enough.

"Uncle?"

Pell waited.

The pause held.

Then his second line came from the same place.

I watched the audience instead of the hanging.

That was my mistake.

Nessa hit my shoulder.

"Tube."

The costume basket had shifted again.

I caught it before it settled onto the leather.

Work.

The ghost continued without me.

After Mourning House, I had eight minutes to become Shopkeeper.

I used six.

The coat button was wrong.

Not broken.

Wrong hole.

I fixed it.

Then I heard applause and thought I had more time than I did.

Teren appeared.

"Go."

"What?"

"Go."

I grabbed the ledger.

My entrance was late.

Not terribly.

Enough.

Marek was already onstage waiting.

He covered.

"At last."

I came in.

"You say that like I wanted to see you."

The audience laughed.

That line was not supposed to be there.

Marek looked pleased.

I hated him.

The rest went fine.

Better than yesterday's first half.

Worse than yesterday's second.

I lost one word and replaced it with another that meant almost the same
thing.

Teren noticed.

Nobody else seemed to.

At the debt turn, a man near the aisle said, "Don't lend him anything."

I looked at Marek.

"Even he understands."

That got more than it deserved.

Afterward, Teren said, "Late."

"I know."

"Why?"

"Ghost."

He looked at me.

"Did it work?"

"Yes."

"Then next time be late for a worse reason."

I laughed.

He didn't.

Maybe a little.

Rinna paid me two copper for the night.

Four copper across two local shows.

That felt small after company silver and large after buying bread.

Money was becoming irritating that way.

Pell got paid too.

Then Rinna took one copper back for the latch.

He protested for three minutes.

Nobody helped him.

I helped Nessa coil the ghost.

That was harder than installing it.

Leather remembered every wrong bend.

"Loose," she said.

"I am loose."

"The coil."

"I know."

"You don't."

I loosened it.

She took the first loop, showed me once, and handed it back.

No speech.

I did the rest.

When we finished, the ghost looked like rope.

That was disappointing.

"Where does it live?" I asked.

"Wall chest."

"With magic?"

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because it's a tube."

"Good."

She looked at me.

"What are you doing?"

"Nothing."

"You're doing the thing."

"What thing?"

"Thinking at props."

"I don't think at props."

"You bought broken magic."

"Pell told you."

"Pell tells everyone everything."

From across the room Pell said, "No I don't."

Nessa ignored him.

I said, "Hessa wants me to write a question."

"Who?"

"Guild."

"The woman?"

"Yes."

"What question?"

"Prepared structure."

Nessa put the ghost into the wall chest.

"Ask someone who makes it."

"I did."

"Then why ask Guild?"

"Different question."

She closed the chest.

"Good."

That was all I got.

Outside, it was properly dark.

The street lamps were lit.

One of the prepared globes near the market had gone green again before
settling yellow. A lamp tender stood beneath it with a long pole and
swore at the fixture.

I walked toward Lyssa's.

She was not there.

The woman downstairs was.

"Road actor."

"Greg."

"Same."

"She's out."

"Where?"

The woman looked at me.

"I don't know."

That answer felt healthy.

"When back?"

"Didn't ask."

Also healthy.

I went upstairs.

Lyssa had told me I could.

That still felt strange.

I ate the end of yesterday's bread.

Then I found paper.

Hessa wanted a question.

I wrote:

HOW MUCH OF THE EFFECT HAS TO BE MINE?

I stared at it.

Wrong.

The blue lamp had gotten into the question again.

I crossed it out.

I wrote:

WHAT IS THE SMALLEST THING I CAN MOVE?

That sounded like a child challenging furniture.

Crossed out.

I wrote:

CAN I PRODUCE A REPEATABLE EXTERNAL CHANGE SMALL ENOUGH TO ISOLATE?

I hated the word isolate.

It sounded like Hessa.

I left it.

Then, underneath:

IF YES, HOW LITTLE OF IT HAS TO CHANGE BEFORE IT COUNTS?

That was worse.

Maybe better.

I did not cross it out.

The door opened downstairs.

Footsteps.

Not Lyssa's.

Someone laughed.

A door closed.

I waited.

Nothing.

I looked at the questions.

Then I remembered Veya's hands stopping around the cloth.

The tube had been real.

Pell's voice had been real.

The dark hanging had been real.

The empty space had contained nothing at all.

I had known that.

I had still looked.

I turned the paper over before I could write something stupid about
ghosts.

Tomorrow I had theatre.

The day after, Hessa had paper.

For now, that was enough.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 178

## THE ENSEMBLE PLAYER

Lyssa came home with somebody else's shoes.

Not wearing them.

Carrying them by the laces.

I was still at the table with Hessa's question facedown when the door
opened and Lyssa came in sideways, one shoulder against the frame, a
paper parcel under one arm and a pair of brown shoes dangling from two
fingers.

She stopped when she saw me.

"You live here now?"

"Apparently."

"Terrible."

"Whose shoes?"

"Jessa's."

"Why?"

"Because she went home barefoot."

"Why?"

Lyssa put the shoes on the table.

"Because her feet hurt."

"That doesn't answer why you have them."

"She left them at Marra's."

"That still doesn't."

"I am returning them tomorrow."

"Now we have a story."

She looked at the paper in front of me.

"What is that?"

"Nothing."

"Guild nothing?"

"Yes."

She reached for it.

I put my hand on top.

"No."

"Then definitely Guild nothing."

"It's a question."

"To who?"

"Hessa."

"The woman who makes you not do magic?"

"She lets me do magic."

"While making you not do magic."

"That's unfair."

"Did anything move?"

"That was yesterday."

Lyssa nodded.

"So no."

"Correct."

She put the parcel beside Jessa's shoes and started unpinning her hair.
The brass leaves were not in it tonight. I noticed that and then felt
stupid for noticing.

"Where were you?"

"Marra's. Then Jessa's sister's. Then the dyer."

"At night?"

"The dyer closes when the work is done."

"What work?"

"Blue."

"That's not work."

"It was six lengths of blue."

"More work."

She opened the parcel.

Inside was cheese.

I respected the parcel more.

"Did you buy that?"

"No."

"Steal it?"

"Payment."

"For blue?"

"For carrying the blue because Jessa took her shoes off."

I looked at the shoes.

"This city has complicated trade."

"You came home with broken magic."

"Educational garbage."

"Where is it?"

I pointed toward my bag.

Lyssa went to the bag.

"No."

She stopped.

"You said it doesn't do anything."

"It doesn't."

"Then why no?"

"Because Hessa said don't alter it."

"I was going to look."

"That's how it starts."

Lyssa stared at me.

Then she laughed.

"You're scared I'll accidentally do magic."

"No."

"You're scared I'll make your trash less educational."

"Yes."

She left the bag alone.

We ate cheese.

Later, she found the question anyway because I forgot it on the table
when I washed.

She read it upside down.

"Can I produce a repeatable external change small enough to isolate?"

"Stop."

"What does that mean?"

"I don't know."

"Good question."

"Give it back."

She did.

Then she read the second line before letting go.

"How little does it have to change before it counts?"

"That's not exactly what it says."

"It's exactly what it says."

"It has more words."

"Why?"

"Hessa."

"Does she charge by the word?"

"No."

"Then you're doing that yourself."

I folded the paper.

"Tomorrow is theatre."

"Today was theatre."

"Tomorrow is also theatre."

"Do you get a day off?"

"I had several before I met them."

"Those don't count."

She was right.

That was annoying.

In bed, I found out she had been using my side for folded clothes.

I moved them.

She moved two back.

"Those are clean."

"So?"

"Your road coat touched the floor in four towns."

"More."

"Exactly."

I put the road coat on the chair.

She moved the clean clothes.

Compromise.

I slept better than I had on the road.

I also woke with Lyssa's elbow in my throat.

Home.

East Market Hall had lost a room overnight.

Not literally.

The room still existed.

A group of six men with rolled papers had rented it.

Rinna was standing in the corridor arguing with one of them.

"I was told noon."

"You were told the room was yours after noon."

"It is after noon."

"It is eleven forty."

Rinna looked toward me.

"What time is it?"

I stopped.

The man looked at me too.

This was dangerous.

"Almost noon."

Rinna smiled.

The man did not.

"Greg," she said, "go away."

I did.

Inside the hall, Pell was repairing the latch.

He had removed it entirely.

"That seems worse."

"It's temporary."

"Door doesn't close."

"That's why it's temporary."

Nessa walked past carrying a painted column.

"Don't talk to him."

"I wasn't."

"You were."

Pell said, "He started it."

Nessa kept walking.

The painted column was stone from ten feet away and wood from two.

I followed it.

Not Nessa.

The column.

She set it beside a shallow doorway built into a painted wall.

The doorway bothered me.

It looked wrong.

The painted wall had lines that narrowed toward the back. The doorway
itself was only deep enough for a person to stand inside and turn
sideways. Somebody had painted another door beyond it.

Up close, the second door was obviously paint.

The floor between them was paint.

The little shadow under the far lintel was paint.

"That's bad," I said.

Nessa looked at me.

"What?"

"The door."

"What door?"

"The back one."

"There is no back one."

"Exactly."

"Good."

"No. It looks fake."

"From here."

She walked away.

I stayed.

Then I went into the seats.

The back door became a door.

Not a good door.

A door.

The real front frame cast an actual shadow across the painted floor. The
painted shadow farther back continued it. The real column hid one edge.
The narrowing lines did the rest.

I moved three seats left.

Worse.

Three seats right.

Better.

Pell appeared beside me.

"What are you doing?"

"Door."

"What?"

I pointed.

He looked.

"That's been there forever."

"I know."

"You've seen it."

"I know."

"Why are you looking now?"

"Go fix your latch."

He left.

I went back to the stage.

There was a wooden crate in front of the column.

I moved it.

The doorway looked more real from here.

Nessa came back.

"Why?"

"Why what?"

"The crate."

"It was blocking the column."

"Put it back."

"Why?"

"Because from the house it blocks the bottom."

"The bottom is real."

"Yes."

"Why hide the real part?"

"Because it looks wrong."

That offended me.

I went back into the seats.

The crate hid where the real floor met the painted floor.

Without it, the seam made the whole thing shallow.

With it, the seam disappeared.

The fake door got deeper.

I put the crate back.

Nessa said nothing.

That was worse than being told.

The day's bill was not yesterday's.

Teren had crossed Shopkeeper out.

I stared at the board.

"What?"

"Not tonight."

"Why?"

"Veya wants the room."

"Veya is not Shopkeeper."

"No."

"What am I?"

"Third Man."

"What is Third Man?"

"Third man."

"How many lines?"

"Seven."

"That's not a role."

"It has a name."

"What name?"

"Third Man."

I looked at him.

He was already reading something else.

"Anything else?"

"Shopkeeper tomorrow."

"Probably?"

"Probably."

I had been demoted by a woman who was not even taking my part.

The piece was called The Petition.

I had seen part of it before we left, but not enough to matter.

Third Man entered with two other petitioners, argued about who had been
waiting longest, delivered a complaint about a goat, and left.

The goat was not present.

Good.

My seven lines were easy.

The problem was that my fifth line was a cue.

Nessa told me that.

Not Teren.

"Don't change it."

"I don't change lines."

She looked at me.

"Not that one."

"Why?"

"Door."

"What door?"

"Side."

She pointed.

A young actor named Sellen was supposed to enter on the word "neighbor."

My line was:

My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience.

Sellen entered on neighbor.

"That's obvious," I said.

"Good."

"Why not enter after goat?"

"Because then he crosses Veya."

"After fence?"

"Music."

"What music?"

"You'll hear it."

I did.

There was a three-note sting from the balcony after fence.

Not magic.

A little reed.

Everything was already full.

We ran it once.

I said the line.

Sellen entered on neighbor.

The reed sounded after fence.

Veya turned.

Nobody hit anyone.

Teren said, "Again."

We did.

Then somebody needed the stage for the rented room's chairs, which did
not make sense until I learned they were borrowing ours.

The six men with rolled papers came through.

One of them pointed at the painted doorway.

"Can that move?"

Nessa said, "No."

"It has wheels."

"No."

"It visibly has wheels."

"No."

They took chairs.

The doorway stayed.

I liked Nessa.

The afternoon broke into pieces.

I carried chairs.

Then costumes.

Then a bucket of paint with a prepared lid that tightened itself when
the rim was pressed twice. Pell pressed it three times and could not
open it.

Nessa made him carry it to the paint woman.

I did not help.

Marek arrived, changed his shirt, ate something from his pocket, and
left again.

"Where are you going?"

"Back."

"Back where?"

He pointed behind himself.

"That's not a place."

"It is if you're going there."

He disappeared through the side door.

I did not see him again until the show.

Serra came in once, spoke to Rinna, took a wrapped bundle from the
office, and left.

She saw me.

"Back?"

"Apparently."

"Good."

That was all.

I wanted to ask where she had been.

I did not.

At four, Lyssa came through the hall carrying Jessa's shoes.

I was holding a painted bench.

"What are you doing?"

"Returning shoes."

"Here?"

"Jessa's sister is meeting me by the west market."

"This is east."

"I know where markets are."

"Why are you here?"

"Shortcut."

She looked at the bench.

"What are you doing?"

"Acting."

"That looks heavy."

"It's a demanding role."

Nessa said from behind me, "Greg."

Lyssa smiled.

"I like her."

"You don't know her."

"I know enough."

She left through the opposite door.

Did not stay.

Did not ask about the show.

Good.

I carried the bench.

By evening, The Petition had changed one chair, two cups, and a coat.

My seven lines had not changed.

I knew them.

That was the problem.

The audience was good.

Not loud.

Interested.

The first petitioner got a laugh I had never heard in rehearsal.

The second got another.

I came in.

We argued.

Veya, playing the clerk, asked what business could possibly justify
three grown men shouting in her office.

The first petitioner answered.

The second answered.

Then me.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Sellen entered.

Perfect.

The audience laughed at the goat.

I should have stopped.

Instead, because the laugh was there and the road had taught me what to
do with a laugh, I looked toward the side door and added:

"And apparently he's followed me."

Bigger laugh.

Good laugh.

Sellen stopped.

Bad.

He had entered as the neighbor's son.

His first line was:

My father sent me because the goat is innocent.

Except I had just implied he was the goat.

The audience looked at him.

Sellen looked at me.

There were several things he could do.

Most were bad.

He chose one.

"My father sent me because the goat is innocent," he said.

The audience laughed again.

Different laugh.

Sellen kept going.

The reed missed its entrance because the balcony player was laughing
too.

Veya waited.

The pause stretched.

Then she slapped the desk.

"Your goat may defend itself after the people."

That was not her line.

It fixed the order.

Sellen moved.

The reed player found the three notes late.

The scene continued.

It worked.

That was the worst part.

Backstage, I was pleased for almost thirty seconds.

Then Sellen came off.

"Don't."

"It worked."

"For you."

There it was.

He was not angry enough to fight.

That would have been easier.

"You entered."

"Yes."

"You covered."

"Yes."

"The audience liked it."

"Yes."

"So..."

He stared at me.

"So I had to become a goat."

I laughed.

He did not.

"Sorry."

"Don't be sorry. Say the line."

"Right."

He walked away.

Teren appeared.

"Good laugh."

I smiled.

"Don't do it again."

Smile gone.

"It worked."

"Sellen already told you why it didn't."

"Yes."

"Good."

He left.

I stood there.

Pell walked past.

"Goat."

"Fuck you."

He laughed.

The next piece used the painted doorway.

I was not in it.

I helped shift the crate.

Then I watched from the side.

Up close, the painted hall beyond the doorway was terrible.

One brushstroke made a wall.

Another made a shadow.

The far door was four dark lines and a brass-colored dot.

An actor crossed through the real frame, stopped where the real floor
ended, and turned as if somebody farther inside had spoken.

He looked into painted space.

The audience looked with him.

Nobody laughed.

The room behind him did not exist.

The crate covered the seam.

The real frame cast the first shadow.

The actor supplied the rest.

I knew that.

I still wanted to see who was in the painted room.

That was becoming a problem.

After the show, Rinna paid me one copper.

"One?"

"Third Man."

"Seven lines."

"Exactly."

"I carried a bench."

"Free."

"Ghost yesterday."

"Different day."

"Door."

"What door?"

I gave up.

One copper.

Still money.

Sellen got paid too.

I considered apologizing again.

Then decided he had specifically told me not to be sorry.

I said, "Neighbor."

He looked at me.

"Goat."

"Fair."

That seemed to fix enough.

Pell was still working on the latch.

The door now closed.

It did not open.

Progress.

Nessa had received a folded note sometime during the second piece. She
read it, put it in her pocket, and left before cleanup finished.

Nobody told me why.

Teren and Veya were arguing quietly near the office.

Not about me.

I could tell because neither looked at me.

That was relaxing.

I moved cups.

Stacked chairs.

Put the crate back where it belonged.

Not where it looked best from the stage.

Where it looked best from the seats.

I was learning which direction mattered.

Outside, Marek was waiting with food.

"For me?"

"No."

He ate it.

"Why are you waiting?"

"Not for you."

"Good."

A woman came around the corner.

Marek handed her a folded paper.

She handed him a small wrapped parcel.

Neither introduced me.

They left in different directions.

I went home.

Lyssa was there this time.

Jessa's shoes were gone.

"Successful?"

"What?"

"The shoes."

"Yes."

"Good."

She was sitting on the floor with cloth spread over her knees, picking
stitches out of one seam.

I put my one copper on the table.

"Rich."

"Third Man."

"What's that?"

"Apparently one copper."

"Good role."

"I was a goat."

She looked up.

I explained.

Not all of it.

Enough.

She laughed harder than the audience had.

"You're horrible."

"It got a laugh."

"At him."

"Yes."

"You're horrible."

"I said sorry."

"Did that help?"

"No."

"Good."

I sat.

The question paper was where I had left it.

Lyssa had put a cup on the corner so it would not curl.

She had not written on it.

I appreciated that.

Tomorrow was Hessa.

I read the question again.

CAN I PRODUCE A REPEATABLE EXTERNAL CHANGE SMALL ENOUGH TO ISOLATE?

Still ugly.

Still probably useful.

I thought about adding something about the doorway.

I did not.

The doorway was not Hessa's problem.

The fact that four painted lines could become a room if one real frame
told the truth first was Nessa's problem.

Maybe nobody's problem.

Maybe just a door.

Lyssa held up the seam she was unpicking.

"Does this look straight?"

"No."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"Because I'm taking it out."

I looked again.

The stitches were very straight.

The cloth underneath them was not.

"Then the stitches are straight."

"Wrong place."

"Oh."

She kept cutting.

I did not say anything else.

Tomorrow Hessa wanted something real to move.

Tonight Lyssa was removing perfectly good stitches because they made the
dress wrong.

At the theatre, a real floor had made a fake room worse until we hid
part of it.

I was beginning to suspect that being technically correct was not as
useful as I had been promised.

That sounded like something Hessa would hate.

I did not write it down.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 179

## THE TESTER

Lyssa was gone before I woke.

There was bread on the table, half a pear, and a note under the cup that
had been holding down my question.

PAPER DAY.

Under that:

DON'T BECOME A GOAT.

I ate the pear.

The question went into my coat.

The failed throw blank did not. I had considered bringing it, then
decided I had already shown Hessa the garbage. Carrying the same useless
piece of metal back to her felt less like research and more like needing
somebody to admire a purchase.

The Guild rooms were busy enough that nobody noticed me for several
minutes.

A man I did not know was standing in the front passage with a cracked
white plate held between both hands. A narrow copper line ran through
its center and stopped at the crack.

"It held yesterday," he said.

A clerk behind the desk said, "It is cracked today."

"Yes."

"So it did not hold today."

"I can see that."

"Good."

I liked the Guild.

Hessa's door was open.

She was not waiting for me.

She had three narrow boxes on her table and a stack of papers under one
elbow. One box was sealed with red wax. One had a little brass tag tied
to it. The third was open and contained six black stones arranged in two
rows.

A woman in a gray Guild coat stood beside her.

"No," Hessa said.

The woman tapped the paper.

"It is the same mark."

"It resembles the same mark."

"How many differences do you need?"

"One useful one."

The woman looked toward me.

"Yours?"

"No," Hessa said.

"Good."

She gathered two papers and left.

Hessa watched her go.

Then she looked at me.

"You have the question?"

I took it out.

She held out her hand.

I gave it to her.

She read the first line.

Then the second.

Then the first again.

"Why are there two?"

"The second is part of the first."

"No."

"Related?"

"Yes."

"That's better."

She put the paper flat on the table.

"Can I produce a repeatable external change small enough to isolate,"
she read. "That is a question."

"Good."

"Do not look pleased."

I stopped.

She tapped the second line.

"If yes, how little of it has to change before it counts."

"Also a question."

"A worse one."

"Why?"

"Counts as what?"

"An effect."

"Observable?"

"Yes."

"Repeatable?"

"Yes."

"Caused by you?"

"Yes."

"Magical?"

I hesitated.

"Hopefully."

Hessa looked at me.

"Those are not one threshold."

"Right."

"You keep trying to make one sentence do several jobs."

"I've been acting."

That came out before I meant it to.

Hessa leaned back slightly.

"How long?"

"What?"

"How long were you with the players?"

"Several weeks."

"And now?"

"Still with them."

"I know."

She pushed the paper back toward me.

"You have spent several weeks being rewarded when people reach the
intended conclusion."

"Sometimes."

"Sometimes the intended conclusion is that Marek is dead."

"That happened."

"Was he dead?"

"No."

"Then stop bringing me conclusions."

I almost laughed.

She did not.

"I wasn't."

"You wrote 'counts.'"

"That's not a conclusion."

"It is asking permission for one."

I folded the paper once.

"Sometimes more real makes something worse."

Hessa's eyes narrowed.

I knew immediately that I should have left that at home.

"Worse at what?"

There it was.

"A play."

"Then ask a player."

"No. I mean, if you're making something look right."

"To an audience."

"Yes."

"Then ask a player."

"Fine."

"Good."

She stood.

"Today we are making something boring."

"I expected that."

"Good."

She moved the three boxes to the far shelf.

"Do not touch those."

"I wasn't going to."

"Good."

The apparatus from the last session was not on the table.

Hessa had changed it.

The shallow wooden frame remained, but the two folded paper tabs were
gone. In their place were two narrow paper fins, each folded once at the
bottom so it could stand upright. They sat between paired wooden guides
no wider than my little finger. Each guide had three ink marks along its
edge.

The glass shield was taller.

It covered the whole frame.

Four little wedges held it off the table.

"What happened to the tabs?"

"They were bad."

"I liked them."

"They were bad."

"Why?"

"Too much surface. Uneven folds. One leaned."

"The target?"

"The control."

"Did that matter?"

"It could have."

"So you changed them."

"Yes."

She put a finger on one paper fin.

"These can move only forward or back without hitting the guides."

"How far?"

"If we are lucky, not at all."

"Right."

"Sit."

I sat.

She turned the frame around.

Then again.

"What are you doing?"

"Annoying you."

"Working."

"That too."

She took two small wooden squares from a cup. One had a dot on the
underside.

She mixed them in her hands and placed one beneath each side of the
frame where I could not see.

"Which is target?"

"You tell me."

"I don't know."

"Good."

"How am I supposed to affect it?"

"You aren't yet."

She lowered the glass.

"First, you draw."

That part had become familiar enough to be dangerous.

I put my hand where she indicated.

Feet settled.

Shoulders loose.

No reaching.

No pushing.

No trying to make the room interesting.

I drew.

The mana came cleanly.

Not large.

Never large.

It gathered with the same internal wrongness that had stopped feeling
entirely wrong. I held the smallest useful amount and stopped.

Hessa watched my face, then my hand.

"Good."

Twenty-two.

I did not say it.

She probably had it written somewhere.

"Now shape."

"Toward what?"

"Nothing."

That was irritating.

I shaped anyway.

Deliberately.

The familiar asymmetry appeared. The wrist edge wanted to become more
definite than the other side. I did not chase it. I held the shape as
evenly as I could.

Hessa walked around the table.

"Again."

"I thought that was one."

"It is."

"Then why again?"

"Because I said again."

I adjusted.

She stopped me before I could rebuild the whole thing.

"Better."

Eighteen.

Maybe.

I still did not say it.

Hessa lifted the glass, reached under the frame, and checked the wooden
squares.

Then she turned the entire frame a quarter turn.

She replaced the glass.

"The left fin."

"That's target?"

"Yes."

"Why hide it before?"

"Because you spent the last session watching paper until you nearly
invented a result."

"I didn't invent it."

"You stopped yourself before you did."

"That's different."

"Yes."

I liked that answer less than I expected.

She pointed to the left fin.

"One direction only. Away from you. Do not move it sideways. Do not lift
it. Do not make it tremble. Do not make it interesting."

"How far?"

"One mark would be excellent."

The marks were tiny.

"That's all?"

Hessa looked at me.

"Move it first."

Fair.

I settled again.

The mana was already there.

I shaped toward the paper.

Not the whole paper.

Not a shove.

That was the problem with thinking move. Move was large. Move contained
success.

I tried to make the intention smaller.

Forward.

Barely.

The room was quiet except for somebody dragging a chair in the passage.

The sound stopped.

I waited.

Nothing happened.

The paper stood between the guides.

I kept the shape.

Nothing.

My leg began to ache from how I was sitting.

I adjusted without thinking.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped.

"What?"

"You moved."

"Me."

"Yes."

"Not the paper."

"Correct."

"Can we try again?"

"We are still trying."

She inspected both fins without touching them.

Neither had moved.

Then she checked the wedges beneath the glass.

"Again."

I reset.

The second time I did not think about the paper.

That was impossible, obviously.

I thought about the space between its front edge and the first ink mark.

Smaller.

The mana held.

The shaping held.

Forward.

The left fin moved.

I saw it.

It did not jump.

It did not fall.

Its bottom edge slid along the wood with a tiny dry sound.

Less than the width of my smallest fingernail.

But it moved.

I stopped breathing.

Hessa said, "Stop."

I stopped everything.

She did not look at me.

She looked at the glass.

Then the right fin.

Then the table.

Then the floor.

"It moved."

Hessa lifted one finger.

I shut up.

She crouched.

Checked the wedges.

Pressed the table with two fingers.

Looked at the paper from the side.

Then she stood.

"Did you touch the table?"

"No."

"Did your knee?"

"No."

"Foot?"

"No."

"I didn't move."

"I know you believe that."

"I know where my foot is."

"Good."

She marked something on the page.

"What did you write?"

"Movement."

"That's it?"

"Yes."

"Target movement?"

"Yes."

"Control?"

"No visible movement."

I felt something open in my chest.

Not mana.

Worse.

Hope.

Hessa saw it.

"Again."

The next attempt did nothing.

Of course.

I held the same shape.

Or I thought I did.

The paper did not move.

The control did not move.

Nothing moved.

"Again," I said.

"No."

"What?"

"Release fully."

"I can do another."

"You can release."

I released.

The mana went.

I hated that.

Hessa waited.

Then she lifted the glass and swapped the fins.

Not the wooden squares.

The fins themselves.

"What are you doing?"

"Seeing if one likes to move."

"Paper doesn't like things."

"Good."

She checked the folds.

One was slightly flatter at the base.

Not much.

Enough that I could see it once she pointed.

"Was that the target?"

"Yes."

My chest closed again.

"So it moved because it was easier."

"I did not say that."

"It could have."

"Yes."

"Then it doesn't count."

Hessa looked at me.

"Counts as what?"

I sighed.

She almost smiled.

Almost.

She turned the frame again.

Then she switched which wooden square sat beneath which side.

I watched.

"Now I know."

"Yes."

"So what's the point?"

"The point is that we are not doing another external attempt."

"What?"

"Not today."

"That was one movement."

"Yes."

"And one failure."

"Yes."

"Which means we need another."

"Which means I need to know whether the apparatus is lying before I ask
you to draw again."

"The apparatus can't lie."

Hessa looked at me.

I thought about painted doors.

"Fine."

"It can mislead."

"Better."

She wrote again.

I leaned.

She covered the page with her hand.

"That's childish."

"Sit back."

I sat back.

"What did you write?"

"Possible directional movement during supervised external attempt. Not
repeated. Apparatus asymmetry identified after attempt."

"Possible."

"Yes."

"It moved."

"Yes."

"Under the glass."

"Yes."

"Control didn't."

"Correct."

"And I was shaping toward it."

"Correct."

"That sounds like magic."

"It sounds like a reason to build a better frame."

I stared at her.

"You hate joy."

"No."

"Evidence?"

"Frequently."

Someone knocked.

Hessa said, "Come."

The woman in the gray coat returned without waiting.

"The mark is on two more."

Hessa stood immediately.

"Where?"

"South storage."

"Both?"

"One crate. Two seals."

"Who opened it?"

"No one."

Hessa looked at me.

"We are done."

"What?"

"You heard her."

"I have theatre later."

"Excellent."

"That's not related."

"I know."

She was already gathering two papers.

"What about next time?"

"Not until I replace the fins."

"When?"

"I will tell you."

"Two days?"

"No."

"Three?"

"Greg."

"Right."

She stopped at the door.

"Do not reproduce this at home."

"I know."

"Do not use different paper."

"I know."

"Do not decide that because one paper moved, you can move paper."

"I wasn't going to."

She waited.

"I was going to a little."

"I know."

The gray-coated woman looked between us.

"Is this the paper man?"

"No," Hessa said.

I said, "Apparently."

Hessa pointed at the door.

I left.

At the front desk, the man with the cracked white plate was gone. The
plate was not. It sat in a shallow tray with a scrap of paper tied to
one corner.

DO NOT USE.

Under that, in different writing:

OBVIOUSLY.

I stopped long enough to read both.

The clerk looked up.

"Yours?"

"No."

"Then keep moving."

I did.

Outside, the day had become offensively normal.

A courier passed with a brass seal at his shoulder that flashed once
when the receiving clerk touched it. A woman was arguing over onions.
Somebody had dropped a basket of laundry in the street.

I had possibly moved paper.

Possibly.

That word was unbearable.

I walked to East Market Hall.

Pell had fixed the latch.

I knew because the door opened.

"Look," he said.

"Congratulations."

"It closes too."

"Magic."

"No."

"Better."

The painted doorway was still there.

The crate was still in front of the seam.

I did not touch it.

Teren had tomorrow's bill half written.

Tonight was mostly rehearsal and a shorter public piece later. I was not
in the public piece.

Good.

Sellen was onstage with The Petition pages.

He saw me.

"Goat."

"Neighbor."

Nessa was not there.

Veya was.

She looked at me.

"You're third again tomorrow."

"Seven lines?"

"Unless you earn fewer."

"Fair."

We ran the entrance.

Veya asked what business justified three grown men shouting in her
office.

First petitioner.

Second petitioner.

Me.

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Sellen entered on neighbor.

The reed sounded after fence.

I said nothing else.

Sellen's eyes flicked toward me.

That was all.

The scene continued.

It felt smaller.

It also worked for everyone.

Afterward, Pell asked why I kept staring at my hand.

"I might have moved paper."

He waited.

"With magic."

He waited longer.

"Maybe."

Pell nodded.

"Good."

"That's it?"

"What do you want?"

"I don't know."

"How far?"

I held my fingers close together.

"Less."

He looked at the gap.

"That's bad magic."

"Apparently."

"Still magic."

"Maybe."

He shrugged.

Then he went to get a coil of rope because somebody had called his name.

I stood alone for perhaps five seconds.

Then Veya shoved a stack of pages into my chest.

"Office."

"What?"

"Take those to Teren."

I took them.

Work.

The public piece that night used no ghost, no blue lamp, no painted
room. It was two people, a table, a bad marriage, and a bowl of onions.

I watched from the side.

The audience laughed in the right places.

One woman cried near the end.

Nothing magical happened.

I thought about the paper anyway.

That was probably why Hessa had sent me away.

At home, Lyssa was not there yet.

I put the question paper back on the table.

Under the second line, I wrote:

ONE MOVEMENT.

Then I stared at it.

I added:

NOT REPEATED.

Then:

ONE FIN WAS EASIER TO MOVE.

That looked worse.

More accurate.

Worse.

I left it.

Lyssa came in while I was taking off my boot.

"Paper day?"

"Yes."

"Did anything move?"

I looked at her.

She stopped.

"Something moved."

"Maybe."

"That's annoying."

"Extremely."

She put down a bundle of dark cloth.

"How much?"

I showed her with my fingers.

She leaned closer.

"That's nothing."

"I know."

She smiled.

"You're happy."

"No."

"Greg."

"Possibly."

She laughed and went to wash her hands.

I looked at the three lines again.

ONE MOVEMENT.

NOT REPEATED.

ONE FIN WAS EASIER TO MOVE.

At the theatre, I could have made a room out of less.

Hessa would not even let me make a result.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
# CHAPTER 180

## THE THIRD MAN

Lyssa had the dark cloth spread across the table when I woke.

It covered breakfast.

"Is there bread under that?"

"No."

"Was there bread under that?"

"Yes."

"What happened to it?"

"I ate it."

I sat up.

Lyssa had pinned one edge of the cloth to itself and was measuring
something with a length of cord. The brass leaves were not in her hair.
They were on the shelf beside the washbasin with two pins through them.

"What is it?"

"Skirt."

"For you?"

"No."

"Marra?"

"No."

"Jessa?"

"No."

She looked at me.

"Am I allowed to know?"

"When I know whether I hate it."

"That seems fair."

She folded the cloth back and uncovered a heel of cheese.

"Breakfast."

"That's not bread."

"You slept."

Apparently that was my fault.

I ate the cheese while she marked the cloth with chalk.

After a while she said, "So paper moved and Hessa says maybe you
didn't."

I stopped chewing.

"That's a hostile summary."

"Is it wrong?"

"The paper definitely moved."

"And maybe you did it."

"Yes."

"Good."

"Why is that good?"

"Because yesterday you said maybe seven times."

"I did not."

"You did."

"You counted?"

"No. I got tired."

She folded the cloth again.

"What does Hessa think?"

"That the frame needs fixing."

"So she thinks the frame moved the paper."

"No."

"She thinks you moved it."

"No."

"She thinks something moved it."

"The paper moved."

Lyssa looked at me.

I pointed at her.

"Exactly."

She laughed.

I finished the cheese.

By the time I left, she had the cloth rolled under one arm and was going
south, not north. I did not ask where. She kissed me once at the door,
told me not to become a magician before supper, and walked away before I
could explain that this was precisely the disputed point.

East Market Hall had acquired a sign.

GREG MOVED PAPER.

It was written in charcoal on the wall beside the repaired latch.

I stood there.

Pell came through the door carrying three wooden bowls.

"Morning."

I pointed.

He looked.

"Oh."

"Did you write that?"

"No."

"Who did?"

"Don't know."

"You told someone."

"Yes."

"Who?"

He thought.

"Several people."

"Why?"

"You moved paper."

"Maybe."

"It moved."

"Yes."

"You were doing magic."

"Yes."

"So."

"No."

Pell shifted the bowls into one hand.

"I don't understand what part you don't understand."

"I don't understand what part you understand."

"Paper moved."

"Yes."

"While you were trying to move it."

"Yes."

"With magic."

"Possibly."

He nodded toward the sign.

"That's too long."

Then he went inside.

I rubbed at the charcoal with my thumb.

It smeared.

The words remained readable.

I rubbed harder.

"Leave it."

Rinna was behind me.

I turned.

"Why?"

"Because somebody will write it again and I don't want charcoal
everywhere."

"It's not true."

"Did paper move?"

"Yes."

"Did you move it?"

"Maybe."

"Then it's badly written."

"Thank you."

"Move chairs."

There were twenty-four folding chairs stacked near the side wall.

I moved chairs.

The hall was busier than it had been on the road and less organized than
I remembered. Two actors I had seen before but never traveled with were
arguing over a coat. A woman with paint on both wrists was repainting
the edge of a window flat because somebody had stored it face-down. Veya
was onstage with Sellen and another man, working through the office
scene without us.

Teren was at the front table talking to a baker.

Not about bread.

"Four evenings," the baker said.

"Three."

"Four."

"Three and the afternoon."

"That's four."

"No."

The baker stared at him.

Teren stared back.

I carried chairs around them.

Nobody asked whether I had moved paper.

That lasted six minutes.

A woman I knew only as one of the costume workers caught my sleeve.

"Pell says you finally did magic."

"No."

Her eyebrows rose.

"Paper moved."

"Yes."

"With magic."

"Maybe."

She looked disappointed.

"What did you do before?"

"Nothing."

"That's worse."

She let go and kept walking.

I found Pell backstage.

"You told her I finally did magic."

"I said you moved paper."

"She heard finally did magic."

"That sounds better."

"It isn't better."

"For a story."

I stopped.

Pell was tying a cord around a bundle of wooden spoons.

He did not notice.

Or he did and did not care.

"For a story," I repeated.

"Yes."

"Hessa would hate you."

"Who?"

"Never mind."

Nessa still was not there.

Her absence had become a practical problem rather than a mystery. Two
costume questions were waiting on a bench with nobody answering them. A
torn cuff had a note pinned to it. The painted doorway needed a strip of
cloth along the back edge, and nobody knew where she had put the right
gray.

Veya knew where the gray was.

"Third shelf."

Pell looked.

"Which room?"

Veya closed her eyes.

"Paint."

"Ah."

He left.

The hall survived.

That was useful to know.

Around noon, Teren put me at the front door with Sellen.

"Why?"

"Because you can speak."

"So can he."

"Not to strangers."

Sellen said, "I can."

Teren looked at him.

Sellen said, "I don't want to."

"See?"

We had a board with the evening bill painted on it.

THE PETITION.

THE WIDOW'S ROOM.

A SHORT MUSICAL PIECE I had never seen.

Two copper at the door for the full bill. One for children. The first
twenty people got the better benches, which seemed less like an
advertisement and more like a threat.

A man stopped.

"Is this the one with the ghost?"

"No," I said.

Sellen said, "Tomorrow."

The man looked interested.

"Real ghost?"

"Yes," I said.

Sellen turned his head.

The man said, "Really?"

"Pell."

"What?"

"The ghost is Pell."

The man looked less interested.

Sellen waited until he had walked away.

"You are bad at this."

"I told the truth."

"You told all of it."

"Apparently that's bad."

"At a door? Yes."

A woman with two children stopped.

"Any animals?"

Sellen said, "A goat."

"There is no goat," I said.

"There is a goat."

"There is discussion of a goat."

"That's a goat."

The children wanted to see the goat.

We sold three seats.

I decided not to interfere.

Later, I helped set the table for The Petition.

The papers on Veya's desk were fake.

Mostly.

The top sheet had six actual lines of writing.

The sheets beneath it had marks that became words from a few paces away
and nothing at all up close.

I picked one up.

"Who writes these?"

Sellen said, "Who cares?"

"Somebody."

"Probably Nessa."

"Nessa writes fake petitions?"

"She does everything."

I put the paper down.

One corner had a real wax seal.

Not a prepared seal.

Just wax.

From the house, the seal made the entire stack look official.

I knew the rest was nonsense.

It still looked more official with the seal.

I did not touch it again.

Before the doors opened, we also had to find a missing bench.

Not repair one. Find one.

Rinna's count said twelve. The hall contained eleven.

Pell counted twice and got thirteen the second time.

"How?"

"I counted that one twice."

"Why?"

"It looked useful."

Sellen found the missing bench in the costume room with three baskets of
hats on it. Nobody knew who had put it there. The hats had to go
somewhere else, which meant a shelf had to be cleared, which meant a box
of old hand props came down.

I ended up holding a wooden knife, two false keys, and a loaf of bread
made from painted cloth.

The bread looked terrible in my hand.

From ten paces away, beside a real bowl and a real knife, it looked like
bread.

I squeezed it.

"Don't," Veya said.

"I'm not hurting it."

"You're making it bread-shaped wrong."

"It is already bread-shaped."

"Not if you crush it."

I put it down.

The real knife on the prop table was dull enough to be safe and heavy
enough to make the fake loaf look more convincing.

I hated noticing that.

"Do we ever use real bread?"

"Yes."

"Why not here?"

"Because this loaf has been dinner for six years."

That was a better answer than anything I had.

We found room for the hats. The bench went out. The audience would never
know any of this had happened, which seemed to be the normal condition
of theatre.

Before the doors opened, Pell had amended the charcoal sign.

GREG MAYBE MOVED PAPER.

That was worse.

"Why did you add maybe?"

"You complained."

"I don't know if this is better."

"It's more accurate."

Rinna passed us.

"Move."

We moved.

The first piece went badly for somebody else.

A stool leg cracked during an entrance and the actor sitting on it
managed to remain upright by grabbing the other actor's sleeve. The
audience laughed. The scene was not funny.

Backstage, nobody cared why they had laughed.

The stool went out.

Another came in.

Work.

Then The Petition.

I stood in the wing and listened to the first petitioner complain about
a drainage ditch.

The second had a pig.

Then Veya called for the third.

I entered.

The local audience was quieter than the road crowds. I knew that now. I
did not throw the first line at them.

Veya looked at me as if I were already wasting her afternoon.

"What grievance?"

"My neighbor's goat has eaten half my fence and all my patience."

Sellen entered on neighbor.

The reed sounded after fence.

There was a laugh.

Small.

Smaller than the laugh I had gotten when I called Sellen a goat.

I felt the old line waiting.

And apparently he's followed me.

It would work.

I knew exactly where to put it.

I did not.

Sellen crossed in, offended.

"My father sent me because the goat is innocent."

The audience laughed harder.

Not at me.

Sellen held the pause.

Then he added, perfectly serious, "My father is less certain."

The laugh got bigger.

Veya looked down at her papers so the audience would not see her mouth
move.

I hated him.

The scene worked.

The reed player hit the next cue.

Veya got her business.

I got my next line.

Nobody had to repair anything.

When we came off, Sellen said, "Better."

"Your father line isn't written."

"No."

"You improvised."

"Yes."

"You told me not to."

"I told you not to ruin my entrance."

"That's different?"

"Very."

He walked away.

I considered killing him.

Not seriously.

Mostly.

Teren caught my shoulder before I could leave the wing.

"Good."

"Sellen improvised."

"I heard."

"He got a bigger laugh."

"Yes."

"I hate this job."

"No, you don't."

He was right, which made it worse.

The Widow's Room used the painted doorway.

I was crew for the change.

The crate stayed where it belonged.

I knew that without being told.

The fake stack of petitions went off. A low table came on. Someone
scattered dust across only the audience-facing half of an old coat and
hung it beside the painted doorway.

I looked at the clean back.

"Why only half?"

The woman with paint on her wrists said, "Dust costs time."

That was all.

From the house, the coat looked abandoned.

From backstage, it looked like somebody had gotten tired halfway through
making it dirty.

The scene did not use the ghost tube.

It did not use magic.

An actor stood beside the painted doorway and spoke into the room that
did not exist.

Nobody answered.

She waited.

The audience waited with her.

Then she closed the real doorframe against the painted dark.

It should not have worked.

It did.

After the bill, Rinna paid me one copper.

"Third."

"Thank you."

She was already counting someone else's share.

"Rinna."

"What?"

"Did Pell tell you I did magic?"

"Yes."

"I didn't."

"Good."

"I might have."

"Bad."

"Why?"
